question: What proportion of adults newly registering with a GP practice have their MMR vaccination history checked and, if unvaccinated or partially vaccinated, are offered catch-up MMR?
why: Measles has re-established endemic transmission risk in the UK when coverage falls, and new registration is a recognised catch-up opportunity that is not systematically used. No closed-loop audit of MMR catch-up at new patient registration has been published in the library.

standard.source: UKHSA Green Book, Measles chapter (updated 2 April 2026)
standard.wording: MMR vaccine can be given to individuals of any age and should be offered opportunistically and promoted to unvaccinated or partially vaccinated younger adults. New GP registration, and entry into college, university or other higher education institutions, prison or military service also provides an opportunity to check an individual's immunisation history. Those who have not received MMR should be offered appropriate MMR immunisation.

population: Adults aged 18 to 45 newly registering with the practice over the audit period. Exclude patients registering only temporarily (less than 3 months) or with a documented allergy contraindicating MMR.
sample: 40 consecutive new adult registrations over the last 3 months, from the practice registration list.
data_source: New patient registration questionnaire, GP record immunisation history (Read/SNOMED codes) and consultation notes.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'MMR history: 0/1/2/unknown' field to the new patient health check template in the EPR, with an automatic task to the practice nurse to offer catch-up MMR whenever fewer than 2 doses are recorded.
reaudit: At 3 months, same template and sample size, on a fresh cohort of new registrations.
close_loop: Present at the practice clinical governance meeting; if the new patient template change raises the rate, keep the mandatory field live and add it to new-partner and locum induction so it is not lost when staff change.
evidence: No closed-loop audit of MMR catch-up at new GP registration has been published in the library.
pitfalls: Immunisation history from other countries is often unavailable → record as 'unknown after checking' rather than assuming fully vaccinated, and offer catch-up unless clear written evidence of 2 doses exists.
Reception staff may not prompt the MMR question at registration → build it into the mandatory new-patient questionnaire, not a free-text box.
Small numbers of eligible unvaccinated adults in some practices → extend the sampling window to 6 months if fewer than 40 new registrations are found.
Staff may worry about vaccine hesitancy conversations taking appointment time → agree a short scripted offer and a nurse-led catch-up clinic slot before cycle 1.
Gains fade once the new-patient template reverts to a free-text field after a system upgrade → re-check the template build after any EPR update.
pearls: Recruit the practice nurse who runs new-patient checks as the change champion before cycle 1.
Agree the catch-up MMR offer script and consent process with the whole team before starting data collection.
Use the same registration list report each cycle so the sample is reproducible.
Link the audit to the practice's outbreak-preparedness discussion to keep it a clinical priority after the lead rotates.
effort: ~25 min per 10 patients from the EPR new-patient template and immunisation record
pass: The new patient health check or registration template records MMR status (two doses, one dose, none or unknown) and, where the patient has had fewer than two documented doses, an offer of catch-up MMR is recorded within 8 weeks of registration.

question: What proportion of severely immunosuppressed adults under 80 who are eligible for shingles vaccination have been offered Shingrix in the last 12 months?
why: Eligibility for shingles vaccination was extended to all severely immunosuppressed adults aged 18 and over in September 2025, but practices commonly identify eligibility only by age band on the immunisation call system. No audit in corpus checks whether immunosuppressed patients outside the routine age cohorts are being offered the vaccine.

standard.source: UKHSA Green Book, Shingles (herpes zoster) chapter (12 August 2025)
standard.wording: From September 2025, Shingrix® should be offered to all severely immunosuppressed individuals aged 18 years and over (with no upper age limit). Previously this was offered to immunosuppressed individuals aged 70 to 79 years and then those aged 50 years and over. Eligible individuals should be offered two doses of Shingrix®.

population: Adults aged 18 to 79 on the practice's severe immunosuppression register (chemotherapy, organ or bone marrow transplant, high-dose steroids, biologic DMARDs, HIV with low CD4 count, or equivalent) not already in the routine age-based shingles cohort. Exclude patients already recorded as having completed a 2-dose Shingrix course.
sample: All patients on the immunosuppression register aged under 80, or 40 consecutive patients if the register is larger, checked over the last 3 months.
data_source: Practice immunosuppression/DMARD register, GP record vaccination history, shingles vaccination call/recall search.

template.note: whether the practice's routine shingles recall found this patient

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a rule-based search that cross-references the immunosuppression/DMARD register against the shingles vaccination record, run monthly by a named administrator, generating a recall letter for anyone not yet offered Shingrix.
reaudit: At 6 months, same register and template.
close_loop: Present at the practice's long-term conditions or prescribing meeting; if the monthly search works, add it to the standing list of automated searches run by the pharmacy technician.
evidence: No audit in corpus of shingles vaccination uptake in immunosuppressed adults outside the routine age cohort.
pitfalls: Age-based call/recall systems will not flag immunosuppressed patients under 50 or 60 → build a separate immunosuppression-register search rather than relying on the age search.
Defining 'severely immunosuppressed' consistently is hard → agree the practice's operational definition (drug list and doses) with a GP before starting.
Small numbers per practice → consider a PCN-level audit pooling several practices.
Clinicians may be unsure about timing relative to chemotherapy cycles → agree a simple rule (for example, avoid the week of chemotherapy) with a specialist in advance.
The immunosuppression register itself may be incomplete → cross-check against recent hospital letters and repeat prescriptions for biologics or high-dose steroids.
pearls: Ask the practice pharmacist to build and run the register cross-reference; they already handle DMARD/biologic searches.
Agree with hospital specialists a simple safe-timing rule for vaccination around treatment before cycle 1.
Use the same immunosuppression register definition at re-audit so the sample is comparable.
Keep the monthly search running after the audit team rotates by assigning it a named permanent owner, not an individual GP.
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from the DMARD/immunosuppression register and vaccination record
pass: The patient's GP record shows a documented offer of Shingrix in the last 12 months (accepted, declined with reason, or already fully vaccinated with 2 doses).

question: What proportion of adults newly added to a pneumococcal at-risk clinical group have been offered pneumococcal vaccination within 3 months of the risk factor being coded?
why: Pneumococcal vaccination for clinical risk groups depends on practices noticing a new diagnosis (for example, starting insulin, a new COPD or chronic kidney disease code) and acting on it, rather than on an age-based call. No audit in corpus checks the time from a new risk-group diagnosis to vaccination offer.

standard.source: UKHSA Green Book, Pneumococcal chapter (29 July 2026)
standard.wording: Adults aged 65 years and over, and clinical risk groups aged 2 years or over: a single dose of 0.5ml of PPV23 or PCV20 ... Antibody levels are likely to decline rapidly in individuals with asplenia, splenic dysfunction (including sickle cell disease) or chronic kidney disease ... and, therefore, re-immunisation with PPV23 or PCV20 is recommended every five years in these groups.

population: Adults aged 18 to 64 with a new qualifying clinical risk group code entered in the last 6 to 9 months, identified from the practice's chronic disease registers. Exclude patients who already had a qualifying risk factor and vaccine before this diagnosis.
sample: 40 consecutive adults with a new qualifying risk-group code over the last 6 months.
data_source: GP clinical coding search (new diagnosis dates), immunisation record, repeat prescription list.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Build an EPR alert that fires when a qualifying risk-group code is entered, creating a task for the practice nurse to check and offer pneumococcal vaccination at the same or next contact.
reaudit: At 6 months, same coding search and template.
close_loop: Present at the practice's QOF/chronic disease review meeting; if the alert increases timely vaccination, keep it enabled for all new risk-group diagnoses, not only the audited ones.
evidence: No audit in corpus of time from new pneumococcal risk-group coding to vaccination offer.
pitfalls: Risk-group coding is often incomplete or inconsistent between clinicians → agree a fixed code list with the coding lead before starting.
Diagnoses made in secondary care may not be coded in primary care promptly → include a check of recent discharge summaries and clinic letters in the search.
Patients may decline vaccination → count a documented, informed decline as meeting the standard.
The 3-month window may be too tight for patients seen infrequently → confirm the window with the team before cycle 1 rather than changing it after seeing the results.
Alert fatigue if too many pop-ups are added to the EPR → restrict the new alert to the specific risk-group codes being audited.
pearls: Ask the practice's data quality lead to build the risk-group code search; it can be reused for other opportunistic vaccination audits.
Agree with the nursing team who owns the task list generated by the alert before go-live.
Use the same code list at re-audit to keep the sample comparable.
Fold the alert into the standard new-diagnosis workflow so it survives staff turnover.
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from the coding search and immunisation record
pass: Pneumococcal vaccine is offered (given, declined with reason, or already up to date) within 3 months of the date the qualifying clinical risk group code (for example, chronic respiratory disease, chronic heart disease, diabetes on medication, chronic kidney disease, chronic liver disease, or immunosuppression) is first entered in the record.

question: What proportion of adults in a pneumococcal high-risk group (asplenia, splenic dysfunction or chronic kidney disease) who are due 5-yearly revaccination receive it within 3 months of the due date?
why: Unlike the once-only PPV23/PCV20 dose for most at-risk adults, asplenia, splenic dysfunction and chronic kidney disease require revaccination every 5 years, a recall step that is easily missed once the initial dose is recorded as complete. No audit in corpus tracks 5-yearly pneumococcal revaccination.

standard.source: UKHSA Green Book, Pneumococcal chapter (29 July 2026)
standard.wording: Antibody levels are likely to decline rapidly in individuals with asplenia, splenic dysfunction (including sickle cell disease) or chronic kidney disease ... and, therefore, re-immunisation with PPV23 or PCV20 is recommended every five years in these groups.

population: All patients on the practice's asplenia, splenic dysfunction or CKD stage 4/5 registers who received a pneumococcal dose 4 years 9 months or more ago. Exclude patients vaccinated within the last 4 years 9 months.
sample: All eligible patients identified by a practice search, or 40 consecutive patients if the register is larger.
data_source: Asplenia/CKD register, immunisation record with vaccination dates.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a 5-year pneumococcal revaccination recall to the practice's existing asplenia/CKD register searches, run quarterly, generating an invitation letter automatically.
reaudit: At 6 months, same registers and template.
close_loop: Present at the practice's long-term conditions meeting; if the quarterly recall works, add it to the standard list of searches run alongside the annual review searches.
evidence: No audit in corpus of 5-yearly pneumococcal revaccination completion in asplenia or CKD patients.
pitfalls: Immunisation records may show the vaccine name but not clearly flag it as needing a 5-year recall → use a dedicated recall date field rather than relying on staff remembering the rule.
Patients may have moved practices since their first dose, losing the vaccination date → request records from PCSE/previous practice where the date is missing.
Small numbers at individual practice level → combine data across a PCN if needed to reach 30-40 cases.
Confusing PPV23 with the routine over-65 dose → clarify in the template that this audit is only about the 5-yearly at-risk revaccination.
Recall lists not reviewed once built → assign a named administrator to run and act on the quarterly search.
pearls: Ask the practice's long-term conditions nurse to lead, since they already run the asplenia/CKD annual review.
Agree the exact due-date calculation (last dose + 5 years) with the whole team before cycle 1.
Use the same register definitions at re-audit for a fair comparison.
Hand the quarterly search to the practice's routine search rota so it continues after the lead moves on.
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from the register and immunisation record
pass: Revaccination is given, or a documented offer and decline is recorded, within 3 months of the 5-year due date calculated from the last dose.

question: What proportion of adult smokers identified in general practice consultations are told about the range of stop-smoking support available and referred if they wish to quit?
why: Brief, opportunistic advice at any contact is the recommended first step in helping people quit, but it depends on smoking status being checked and acted on, not just recorded. No closed-loop general practice audit of opportunistic stop-smoking referral (as opposed to hospital admission NRT prescribing) has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG209 Tobacco: preventing uptake, promoting quitting and treating dependence, rec 1.12.1 (2021, amended 2025)
standard.wording: Tell people who smoke that a range of interventions is available to help them stop smoking. Explain how to access them and refer people to stop-smoking support if appropriate.

population: Adults attending a GP or practice nurse appointment for any reason, with current smoking status recorded in the last 12 months. Exclude patients recorded as never-smokers or long-term ex-smokers.
sample: 40 consecutive current-smoker consultations over the last 4 weeks, from a search of coded smoking status.
data_source: Consultation notes, smoking status Read/SNOMED code, referral letters to stop-smoking services.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a one-click 'discussed stop-smoking support / referred' template item to the consultation screen that pops up whenever the smoking status is 'current smoker', linked directly to the local stop-smoking service referral form.
reaudit: At 3 months, same coded search and template.
close_loop: Present at the practice meeting; if the template prompt increases referral rates, keep it live for every consultation type, not only specific clinics.
evidence: No closed-loop general practice audit of opportunistic stop-smoking referral has been published in the library.
pitfalls: Smoking status may be out of date → include a rule to re-check status if it has not been updated in 12 months.
Staff may feel repeated advice annoys patients → agree brief, non-judgemental wording in advance, as NICE recommends.
Recording bias: 'discussed' may be ticked without a genuine conversation → spot-check a sample of consultation free text alongside the coded box.
Referral pathways to external stop-smoking services vary by area and may be confusing → print the local referral route on the consultation template before cycle 1.
Improvement may fade once the prompt becomes routine and is dismissed automatically → review click-through rates at re-audit, not just referral numbers.
pearls: Recruit the practice's health promotion or long-term conditions lead to champion the template change.
Agree the referral pathway and paperwork with the local stop-smoking service before cycle 1.
Keep the same coded smoking-status search for both cycles so results are comparable.
Report referral numbers back to reception and nursing staff regularly to sustain motivation after the lead moves on.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the consultation record and coded smoking status
pass: The consultation record shows smoking status was checked, the patient (if a current smoker) was told about the range of stop-smoking options, and, if the patient expressed interest, a referral to stop-smoking support (in-house, pharmacy or specialist service) was made or offered.

question: What proportion of adults who screen positive for hazardous or harmful drinking on AUDIT/AUDIT-C in general practice receive a structured brief alcohol intervention at the same or next contact?
why: Screening without a structured brief intervention delivers little benefit, and delivery of the FRAMES-based brief advice step is rarely measured separately from screening completion. No audit in corpus of alcohol brief intervention delivery (as opposed to screening rate) has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE PH24 Alcohol-use disorders: prevention, Recommendation 10: brief advice for adults (2010)
standard.wording: Offer a session of structured brief advice on alcohol. If this cannot be offered immediately, offer an appointment as soon as possible thereafter. Use a recognised, evidence-based resource that is based on FRAMES principles (feedback, responsibility, advice, menu, empathy, self-efficacy). It should take 5–15 minutes.

population: Adults with a new AUDIT or AUDIT-C score in the hazardous or harmful range (AUDIT 8-19 or AUDIT-C ≥5) recorded in the last 3 months. Exclude patients scoring in the possible dependence range (AUDIT ≥20) who need a full assessment rather than brief intervention.
sample: 40 consecutive patients with a new hazardous/harmful AUDIT or AUDIT-C score over the last 3 months.
data_source: AUDIT/AUDIT-C coded score, consultation notes, NHS Health Check template, referral records.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'brief intervention delivered / appointment offered' field to the AUDIT/AUDIT-C template, which cannot be closed until completed, and give staff a standard FRAMES-based script card.
reaudit: At 3 months, same coded search and template.
close_loop: Present at the practice's health promotion meeting; if the mandatory field improves delivery, keep it in the NHS Health Check and new-patient templates permanently.
evidence: No audit in corpus of structured brief alcohol intervention delivery after a positive AUDIT/AUDIT-C in general practice.
pitfalls: Screening and brief intervention may both be ticked as done without a genuine 5-15 minute conversation → spot-check free-text notes against the coded box.
Appointment time pressure may push staff to skip the intervention → build a 10-minute brief-intervention slot into nurse or HCA clinics.
Patients scoring in the possible-dependence range need a different pathway (full assessment, not brief intervention) → exclude them from this audit and route separately.
Staff training in FRAMES-based brief advice varies → agree and circulate one resource before cycle 1.
Improvement may fade if the template field becomes a routine tick-box → review free-text quality at re-audit.
pearls: Recruit a practice nurse or HCA trained in alcohol brief intervention to champion the change.
Agree the FRAMES-based resource and script with the whole team before starting data collection.
Use the same AUDIT/AUDIT-C threshold definitions at re-audit for a fair comparison.
Keep the mandatory template field live after the audit team rotates by building it into new-starter induction.
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from the AUDIT template and consultation notes
pass: A structured brief alcohol intervention (using a FRAMES-based resource, taking 5-15 minutes) is delivered at the same appointment, or an appointment for one is offered within 2 weeks, for every patient scoring in the hazardous or harmful range on AUDIT or AUDIT-C.

question: What proportion of women reaching the 20-week screening scan in pregnancy have been offered pertussis vaccination, and what proportion have received it before 32 weeks?
why: Pertussis vaccination in pregnancy protects newborns before they are old enough for their own vaccine course, but protection is reduced if given after 32 weeks. No audit in corpus of the timing of pertussis vaccination in pregnancy (as opposed to overall uptake) has been published in the library.

standard.source: UKHSA Green Book, Pertussis chapter (19 December 2025)
standard.wording: Pregnant women should be offered a single 0.5 ml dose of pertussis containing vaccine in every pregnancy. Women should normally receive pertussis vaccine around the time of the mid-pregnancy scan (usually 20 weeks) but can receive it from 16 weeks gestation. To maximise the likelihood that the baby will be protected from birth, the vaccine should be given before 32 weeks.

population: Pregnant women booked with the practice who reached their 20-week scan in the last 3 months. Exclude women who transferred care from another practice after 20 weeks.
sample: 40 consecutive women reaching 20 weeks over the last 3 months, from the practice maternity register.
data_source: GP maternity template, antenatal records shared from the maternity unit, immunisation record.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic 'pertussis vaccine due' task to the GP maternity template at the point the 16-week booking bloods are recorded, with a reminder if not given by the time the 20-week scan result is filed.
target: ≥90% offered by 20 weeks; ≥85% vaccinated before 32 weeks
reaudit: At 6 months, same maternity register and template.
close_loop: Present at the practice's maternity/perinatal meeting; if the reminder task improves timing, extend it to cover whooping cough vaccine alongside the flu vaccine reminder for pregnant patients.
evidence: No audit in corpus of pertussis vaccination timing relative to 32 weeks in pregnancy.
pitfalls: Vaccination may be delivered by the maternity unit rather than the GP practice, so records can be incomplete in the GP system → cross-check with the hand-held maternity notes or shared care record.
Some women decline vaccination → record a documented, informed decline as distinct from a missed offer.
Late bookers may reach 20 weeks with little time before 32 weeks → flag these women for an earlier offer at booking.
Coding of pregnancy stage may be inconsistent → agree a standard gestation-recording method before starting.
Improvement may not persist if midwifery and GP records are not integrated → confirm information-sharing arrangements with the maternity unit before cycle 1.
pearls: Recruit the practice's maternity liaison midwife or lead GP to champion the reminder task.
Agree with the local maternity unit how vaccination given there will be recorded back in the GP system.
Use the same maternity register extraction method at re-audit.
Keep the reminder task linked to the booking bloods step so it continues automatically after the audit lead moves on.
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from the maternity template and immunisation record
pass: Pertussis vaccination is offered at or before the 20-week scan appointment and, where accepted, is given before 32 weeks of gestation.

question: What proportion of patients on the practice's non-responder list for cervical screening have a documented follow-up action recorded within 8 weeks of appearing on the list?
why: The national call and recall system generates a non-responder list after an invitation and reminder go unanswered, but what a practice then does with that list is locally variable and rarely measured. No closed-loop audit in corpus targets non-responder follow-up specifically (as opposed to colposcopy follow-up, which NNA-342 already covers).

standard.source: NHS Cervical Screening: guidance for call and recall administration best practice, section 10 (updated 2024)
standard.wording: Individuals join the non-responder list (NRL) if they have been sent an invitation and a reminder but have not attended for a test within 26 weeks of their NTDD (or 32 weeks of invite). GP practices will be prompted to check their NRL on CSMS.

population: Women and people with a cervix aged 25 to 64 appearing on the practice's cervical screening non-responder list in the last 3 months. Exclude patients already formally ceased from the screening programme.
sample: 40 consecutive patients added to the non-responder list over the last 3 months, or all if fewer.
data_source: Cervical Screening Management System (CSMS) non-responder list, GP record, call/recall search.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Assign a named administrator to review the CSMS non-responder list monthly and action every entry within 2 weeks, using an agreed local script for calls and opportunistic flags.
reaudit: At 3 months, same non-responder list source and template.
close_loop: Present at the practice meeting; if monthly review closes the gap, add it to the practice's standing list of monthly administrative tasks.
evidence: NNA-342 (colposcopy follow-up) is a related but distinct audit; no closed-loop audit of cervical screening non-responder list follow-up has been published in the library.
pitfalls: The non-responder list may not be checked regularly if no one owns the task → name a specific administrator and add it to their job plan before cycle 1.
Opportunistic flags may be added but never actioned at the next visit → audit whether the flag led to a discussion, not just whether it was added.
Patients who have valid reasons for non-attendance (for example, no cervix, pregnancy) should be excluded or ceased, not repeatedly chased → build a clear ceasing pathway.
Data protection and consent must be respected for phone calls → confirm the practice's telephone contact policy before starting.
Improvement may fade if the CSMS list is not checked after the administrator changes role → document the process in a standard operating procedure.
pearls: Recruit the practice's screening administrator as the audit lead, since they already access CSMS.
Agree a short call script and letter template addressing common barriers (fear, embarrassment, cultural sensitivity) before cycle 1.
Use the same CSMS extraction method at re-audit for a fair comparison.
Write the monthly review into a standard operating procedure so it survives staff changes.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from CSMS and the GP record
pass: Within 8 weeks of a patient appearing on the practice's cervical screening non-responder list, the record shows a documented follow-up action: a further invitation, a phone call, a discussion opportunistically flagged for the next appointment, or a recorded reason for ceasing recall.

question: What proportion of patients eligible for an NHS Health Check who do not attend their first invited appointment are re-invited using a different contact method within 12 weeks?
why: The NHS Health Check programme is designed as a rolling 5-year offer to the whole eligible population, but a single unanswered invitation often leads to no further contact until the next scheduled call. No audit in corpus of NHS Health Check non-attender re-invitation has been published in the library.

standard.source: NHS Health Check generic service specification for general practice (NHS Health Check programme, Public Health England template)
standard.wording: The check is offered once every five years. The Department of Health expects 20% of the eligible population to be invited each year over the 5 year rolling programme with an uptake moving from an initial 50% towards 75%... The practice will ensure that the most appropriate mix of invitation methods are used to encourage uptake of the programme... All attempts to contact patients will be recorded using the agreed local template. DNAs should be managed in line with the practice's own local DNA policy.

population: Adults aged 40 to 74, eligible for an NHS Health Check, who did not attend their first invited appointment in the last 6 months. Exclude patients who have since had a Health Check or become ineligible (for example, new CVD diagnosis).
sample: 40 consecutive DNAs to a first NHS Health Check invitation over the last 6 months.
data_source: NHS Health Check invitation log, appointment system, GP record.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Build a 12-week DNA recall rule into the NHS Health Check invitation system that automatically triggers a second invitation by a different method (text after a letter, or a phone call after a text).
reaudit: At 6 months, same invitation log and template.
close_loop: Present at the practice's public health/QOF meeting; if the automatic recall rule works, keep it as the default DNA pathway for all Health Check invitations.
evidence: No audit in corpus of NHS Health Check DNA re-invitation using a different contact method.
pitfalls: DNA management is often left to individual staff discretion → write a single agreed local DNA policy before cycle 1.
Contact details may be out of date, especially for less engaged groups → verify phone numbers at the point of first invitation.
Practices may deprioritise Health Checks against same-day clinical demand → protect specific appointment slots for the programme.
Equity: some groups (deprived, hard-to-reach) DNA more often and need tailored, not just repeated, invitations → review DNA rates by deprivation decile if data allow.
Improvement may fade once the automatic rule is switched off after a system change → check the rule is still active at re-audit.
pearls: Recruit the healthcare assistant or nurse who runs the Health Check clinic to lead the audit.
Agree the second-contact method and script with reception before cycle 1.
Use the same invitation log extraction method at re-audit for a fair comparison.
Report DNA and re-invitation rates to the practice manager regularly to keep the recall rule prioritised after the lead rotates.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the invitation log and appointment system
pass: A patient who does not attend their first invited NHS Health Check appointment is re-invited using a different contact method (for example, phone call or text after a letter) within 12 weeks, with the attempt recorded on the practice's invitation log.

question: What proportion of people entering prison have a first-stage health assessment completed, before allocation to a cell, that documents any prescribed medicines and immediate health and safety issues?
why: The first-stage assessment is meant to happen before cell allocation so that continuity of medicines and urgent risks are identified immediately, but delays under operational pressure at reception are a recognised risk. No audit in corpus of first-stage prison reception health assessment completion before cell allocation has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG57 Physical health of people in prison, rec 1.1.1 (2016)
standard.wording: At first reception into prison, a healthcare professional (or trained healthcare assistant under the supervision of a registered nurse) should carry out a health assessment for every person. Do this before the person is allocated to their cell. As part of the assessment, identify: any issues that may affect the person's immediate health and safety before the second-stage health assessment; priority health needs to be addressed at the next clinical opportunity.

population: All new receptions into the prison (first reception, not transfers already assessed elsewhere) over the audit period. Exclude same-day court returns already assessed that day.
sample: 40 consecutive new receptions over the last 4 weeks, from the reception log.
data_source: Prison electronic health record (SystmOne or equivalent), reception log, cell allocation record.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Make cell allocation on the prison IT system dependent on the first-stage health assessment record being saved first, so custodial staff cannot allocate a cell before healthcare confirms the assessment is complete.
reaudit: At 3 months, same reception log and template.
close_loop: Present to the prison health and justice governance board; if the system dependency works, embed it as a standard operating procedure across the health and justice contract.
evidence: No audit in corpus of first-stage prison reception assessment completion before cell allocation.
pitfalls: Late-night or high-volume receptions create time pressure that can push assessment after cell allocation → agree an escalation process for surge nights before cycle 1.
Custody and healthcare IT systems may not talk to each other, making the sequencing hard to verify → use manual timestamp checks if systems are not linked.
Staff may complete the assessment but backdate or forget to timestamp it → audit against the reception log time, not just presence of a record.
Reduced staffing at weekends and bank holidays → review results by day of week to check for a pattern.
The IT dependency change needs governor and healthcare provider sign-off together → secure both before cycle 1, not after.
pearls: Recruit the reception nurse lead and the prison's head of residence together, since this crosses healthcare and custodial systems.
Agree the IT change with both the healthcare records supplier and the prison establishment before cycle 1.
Use the same reception log extraction at re-audit for a fair comparison.
Report results at the joint health and justice partnership board so the change survives staff and contract rotation.
effort: ~20 min per 10 receptions from the prison health record and reception log
pass: The first-stage health assessment (Table 1 of NG57) is completed and documented before the person is recorded as allocated to a cell, including the prescribed-medicines question and identification of any immediate health and safety issues.

question: What proportion of people in prison have a second-stage health assessment completed within 7 days of their first-stage assessment?
why: The second-stage assessment covers substance misuse history, sexual health, family history and screening history that cannot always be completed at first reception, and delay increases the risk that treatable conditions and screening gaps go unaddressed. No audit in corpus of second-stage prison health assessment timeliness has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG57 Physical health of people in prison, rec 1.1.13 (2016)
standard.wording: A healthcare professional (for example, a registered general nurse) should carry out a second-stage health assessment for every person in prison. Do this within 7 days of the first-stage health assessment.

population: All people in prison who had a first-stage health assessment in the last 6 weeks, allowing enough time to have reached the 7-day deadline. Exclude people released or transferred before day 7.
sample: 40 consecutive receptions with a completed first-stage assessment over the last 6 weeks.
data_source: Prison electronic health record, reception log.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic 'second-stage assessment due' task to the prison health record, created on completion of the first-stage assessment with a 7-day countdown visible on the nursing team's daily worklist.
reaudit: At 3 months, same reception log and template.
close_loop: Present to the prison health and justice governance board; if the automatic worklist task works, extend it to all reception pathways across the health and justice contract.
evidence: No audit in corpus of second-stage prison health assessment completion within 7 days.
pitfalls: Staff shortages on the nursing team can push second-stage assessments beyond 7 days → review staffing rotas alongside the audit results.
People released or transferred within 7 days will not have a completed second-stage assessment for a valid reason → exclude them rather than counting as a failure.
IT worklists may not be checked if not part of the daily routine → build the check into the nursing handover, not a separate report.
Assessment quality may drop if teams rush to hit the 7-day target → spot-check a sample of second-stage assessments for completeness alongside timeliness.
Improvement may fade if the worklist task is not maintained after an IT upgrade → confirm it is still functioning at re-audit.
pearls: Recruit the prison's senior nurse for reception healthcare as the audit lead.
Agree the worklist design with the nursing team before cycle 1 so it fits their existing handover process.
Use the same reception log extraction method at re-audit.
Review the worklist task list at the weekly clinical governance meeting so it stays visible after the audit team changes.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the prison health record
pass: The second-stage health assessment is completed and documented within 7 days (168 hours) of the recorded date and time of the first-stage assessment.

question: What proportion of people entering prison who were taking prescribed medicines in the community have their next dose confirmed as given, or a prescriber referral made, before the second-stage health assessment?
why: Missed or delayed doses of critical medicines on reception into prison are a recognised source of preventable harm, but continuity depends on rapid communication between reception staff and the prescriber. No audit in corpus of medicines continuity from reception to second-stage assessment has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG57 Physical health of people in prison, recs 1.1.4 (table 1, item 2) and 1.7.10 (2016)
standard.wording: [Prescribed medicines] Yes: document any current medicines being taken and generate a medicine chart. Refer the person to the prescriber for appropriate medicines to be prescribed, to ensure continuity of medicines. If medicines are being taken, ensure that the next dose has been provided... Let the person know that medicines reconciliation will take place before the second-stage health assessment. [1.7.10] Ensure the person can keep taking their medicines after coming into prison.

population: All new receptions who reported taking one or more prescribed medicines at first-stage assessment over the audit period. Exclude people reporting only over-the-counter creams or drops with no ongoing prescription need.
sample: 40 consecutive receptions reporting prescribed medicines over the last 4 weeks.
data_source: Prison electronic health record, medicine chart, reception log.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Build a same-day electronic referral from the reception nurse's medicines question directly to the prison pharmacist/prescriber worklist, with a flag that clears only once the next dose is confirmed given.
reaudit: At 3 months, same reception log and template.
close_loop: Present to the prison medicines optimisation committee; if the electronic referral closes the gap, embed it as the standard reception medicines pathway.
evidence: No audit in corpus of medicines continuity from prison reception to second-stage assessment.
pitfalls: Community medication lists brought in by the person may be incomplete or unverifiable → agree a process for contacting the community pharmacy or GP the same day.
Critical medicines (for example, anticonvulsants, insulin, opioid substitution therapy) need faster action than routine ones → prioritise these using the NG57 table 2 critical medicines list.
Reception nights with high volume may overwhelm the pharmacist worklist → agree an escalation and cover plan before cycle 1.
Paper-based medicine charts can be lost between reception and the wing → track the chart alongside the person, not as a separate document.
Improvement may fade if the electronic referral is bypassed during IT downtime → have a clear paper backup process and check it is used correctly at re-audit.
pearls: Recruit the prison pharmacist and reception nurse lead jointly, since this spans both roles.
Agree escalation routes for out-of-hours prescribing before starting data collection.
Use the same critical-medicines definition (NG57 table 2) at re-audit.
Report near misses as well as full audit results to keep the pathway prioritised after the lead rotates.
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from the prison health record and medicine chart
pass: For a person who reports taking prescribed medicines at first-stage assessment, the record shows either the next dose was given/provided, or a same-day referral to the prescriber was made, and full medicines reconciliation is completed before or at the second-stage assessment.

question: What proportion of people in prison who were on community opioid substitution treatment have their opioid substitution medicine continued, at a confirmed dose, within 24 hours of reception?
why: Interruption of opioid substitution treatment on reception into prison is a recognised cause of withdrawal, illicit drug-seeking and fatal overdose risk on release, yet confirming the community dose and pharmacy before the first inpatient dose depends on rapid cross-checking that is easy to miss under reception pressure. No audit in corpus of opioid substitution continuity specifically at prison reception has been published in the library (NNA-162 covers psychiatric ward admission, not prison reception).

standard.source: NICE NG57 Physical health of people in prison, recs 1.1.4 (table 1, item 14) and 1.7.10-1.7.11 (2016)
standard.wording: [Alcohol and substance misuse] Has the person used street drugs in the last month?... heroin, methadone... Yes: refer the person to substance misuse services if there are concerns about their immediate clinical management and they need immediate support... [1.7.10] Ensure the person can keep taking their medicines after coming into prison. [1.7.11] Give critical medicines in a timely way to prevent harm from missed or delayed doses [including] drugs used to treat substance misuse.

population: All new receptions who report current opioid substitution treatment at first-stage assessment over the audit period. Exclude people who report having already stopped OST more than 4 weeks previously.
sample: 40 consecutive receptions reporting current OST over the last 6 weeks, or all if fewer.
data_source: Prison substance misuse service record, reception log, community pharmacy confirmation record.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a same-day electronic confirmation pathway between the prison substance misuse team and community pharmacies (or the national controlled drug database where available), with a target of confirming dose and pharmacy within 4 hours of reception.
reaudit: At 3 months, same reception log and template.
close_loop: Present to the prison substance misuse governance meeting; if the confirmation pathway closes the gap, embed it in the health and justice service specification for the establishment.
evidence: No audit in corpus of opioid substitution treatment continuity at prison reception (distinct from NNA-162, which covers psychiatric ward admission).
pitfalls: Community pharmacies or prescribers may be unreachable out of hours or at weekends → agree an escalation and interim-dose protocol with clinical leadership before cycle 1.
Self-reported doses may be inaccurate or exaggerated → always attempt independent confirmation before prescribing the full dose.
Reception at night or on Fridays increases delay risk → review results by day/time of reception.
Prescribers may be reluctant to prescribe without full confirmation, causing safe but slow practice → agree a documented interim bridging protocol for uncertain cases.
Improvement may fade if the confirmation pathway relies on one enthusiastic clinician → build it into the substance misuse team's standard operating procedure.
pearls: Recruit the prison substance misuse lead clinician and the reception nurse team together.
Agree the interim bridging protocol and escalation contacts with the substance misuse service before cycle 1.
Use the same OST-reporting definition at re-audit.
Report near-miss delays as well as completed audits at the substance misuse governance meeting to sustain the pathway after staff turnover.
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from the substance misuse record and reception log
pass: For a person confirmed to be on community methadone or buprenorphine, the substance misuse team confirms the dose and last dispensing with the community pharmacy/prescriber, and a dose is prescribed and given within 24 hours of reception.

question: What proportion of people entering prison are offered confidential testing for hepatitis B and hepatitis C, and what proportion of those tested receive their result regardless of location?
why: Prisons are a key opportunity to find and treat blood-borne viruses in a population with higher prevalence and poorer community access to testing, but opt-out or offered testing at reception is not always completed or results relayed if the person moves location. No audit in corpus of hepatitis B/C testing offer and result delivery at prison reception has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG57 Physical health of people in prison, recs 1.1.23 (2016), adapted from the NICE guideline on hepatitis B and C testing
standard.wording: Prison healthcare services (working with the NHS lead for hepatitis) should ensure that: all people are offered a hepatitis B vaccination when entering prison... all people are offered access to confidential testing for hepatitis B and C when entering prison and during their detention; people who test for hepatitis B or C receive the results of the test, regardless of their location, when they become available.

population: All new receptions over the audit period. Exclude people who can show a documented negative test result from within the last 3 months elsewhere.
sample: 40 consecutive new receptions over the last 4 weeks.
data_source: Prison electronic health record, blood-borne virus testing register.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add hepatitis B/C testing as a default opt-out item on the first-stage reception assessment template, with an electronic result-tracking flag that stays open (and is checked at every wing move or segregation transfer) until the result is confirmed given to the patient.
target: ≥90% offered; ≥95% of those tested given their result
reaudit: At 3 months, same reception log and testing register.
close_loop: Present to the prison health and justice governance board; if the opt-out default and tracking flag work, embed them in the establishment's standard reception pathway and health and justice contract KPIs.
evidence: No audit in corpus of hepatitis B/C testing offer and result delivery at prison reception.
pitfalls: People may be transferred or released before results are back → build a handover process that follows the result, not just the person's location on the day of testing.
Opt-out testing still requires informed consent and cultural sensitivity → agree a standard explanation script before cycle 1.
Segregation or healthcare in-patient status can make results harder to deliver in person → include a specific check for these locations in the tracking flag.
Laboratory turnaround delays are outside the practice's control → report delays separately from delivery failures.
Improvement may fade if the electronic flag is closed prematurely → spot-check a sample of 'result given' entries against actual documented conversations.
pearls: Recruit the prison's blood-borne virus lead nurse and NHS hepatitis lead jointly.
Agree the opt-out script and consent process with the whole reception team before cycle 1.
Use the same reception log extraction method at re-audit.
Report testing and result-delivery rates to the health and justice partnership board so the pathway survives contract and staff changes.
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from the prison health record and BBV testing register
pass: The record shows hepatitis B and C testing was offered at reception, and, where the person accepted and was tested, the result was documented as communicated to the person regardless of their current location (including segregation or transfer).

question: What proportion of people entering prison are offered an HIV test at reception?
why: HIV testing at prison reception identifies undiagnosed infection in a population at higher risk with historically poorer community testing access, but the offer depends on it being a routine, non-optional part of the reception pathway rather than left to individual judgement. No audit in corpus of HIV testing offer rates at prison reception has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG57 Physical health of people in prison, rec 1.1.24 (2016), adapted from the NICE guideline on HIV testing
standard.wording: Offer all people HIV testing when entering prison.

population: All new receptions over the audit period. Exclude same-day court returns already tested that day.
sample: 40 consecutive new receptions over the last 4 weeks.
data_source: Prison electronic health record, blood-borne virus testing register.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Combine the HIV test offer with the hepatitis B/C offer as a single mandatory blood-borne virus testing block on the first-stage reception template, so none of the three can be skipped independently.
reaudit: At 3 months, same reception log and template.
close_loop: Present to the prison health and justice governance board; if the combined testing block improves the offer rate, keep it as the default reception pathway and report the rate as a standing health and justice KPI.
evidence: No audit in corpus of HIV testing offer rates at prison reception.
pitfalls: Staff may assume HIV testing is only needed for people reporting risk factors, contrary to the opt-out approach recommended → make it a default with reasoned opt-out, not opt-in.
Stigma concerns may make some staff hesitant to raise the offer routinely → provide brief training and a standard script before cycle 1.
Reception time pressure can push non-mandatory items to be skipped → make the combined BBV block a required field before the assessment can be saved.
Repeat testing of people known to be already diagnosed wastes capacity → exclude them clearly in the template.
Improvement may fade if the mandatory field is later made optional in an IT update → confirm the field remains mandatory at re-audit.
pearls: Recruit the prison's blood-borne virus lead nurse as the audit lead, combining this with the hepatitis B/C audit for efficiency.
Agree a brief non-stigmatising offer script with the whole reception team before cycle 1.
Use the same reception log extraction method at re-audit.
Report the combined BBV testing rate at the health and justice partnership board to keep it prioritised after staff turnover.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the prison health record
pass: The reception health record documents that an HIV test was offered, with the outcome recorded (accepted and tested, declined, or already known positive/negative within 3 months).

question: What proportion of people in prison, or at prisons receiving from high-incidence areas, who are under 65 and in regular contact with substance misuse services are offered an interferon-gamma release assay for TB, combined with hepatitis B/C and HIV testing?
why: TB screening in prisons is recommended alongside blood-borne virus testing for people in contact with substance misuse services, but the two are often organised by separate teams and one can be completed without the other. No audit in corpus of combined TB/BBV testing in this group has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG33 Tuberculosis, recs 1.2.3.5 and 1.2.3.6 (2012, amended 2016)
standard.wording: In high incidence areas (and at prisons that receive prisoners from high incidence areas), prison health services should offer an interferon-gamma release assay for TB to inmates younger than 65 years who are in regular contact with substance misuse services or other support services... Substance misuse services and prison health services should incorporate interferon-gamma release assay testing with screening for hepatitis B and C, and HIV testing.

population: People under 65 engaged with the prison substance misuse service over the audit period, at an establishment identified as receiving prisoners from TB high-incidence areas. Exclude people with a documented active or recently treated TB episode.
sample: 40 consecutive substance misuse service attendees under 65 over the last 3 months, or all if fewer.
data_source: Substance misuse service record, TB screening register, blood-borne virus testing register.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a single combined 'blood-borne virus and TB testing' order set to the substance misuse service's clinical template so IGRA, hepatitis B/C and HIV testing are requested together by default.
reaudit: At 3 months, same service record and template.
close_loop: Present at the joint TB/substance misuse governance meeting; if the combined order set works, extend it to all substance misuse service contacts across the establishment.
evidence: No audit in corpus of combined TB IGRA and blood-borne virus testing in prison substance misuse service attendees.
pitfalls: TB screening and BBV testing are often commissioned and delivered by separate teams → agree a single combined pathway and blood-draw process before cycle 1.
Establishing whether a prison 'receives from high incidence areas' needs local public health input → confirm this with the local TB team before starting.
Support for continuing treatment after release is a precondition in the NICE recommendation → confirm community follow-up arrangements are in place before offering testing.
Substance misuse service attendance is often episodic → use the first contact in the audit period as the index event, not every subsequent contact.
Improvement may fade if the combined order set reverts to separate requests after an IT change → check it remains combined at re-audit.
pearls: Recruit the substance misuse lead nurse and the multidisciplinary TB team jointly, since NICE requires their integration.
Confirm continuity-of-care arrangements for post-release treatment before cycle 1, as NICE specifies.
Use the same substance misuse service contact definition at re-audit.
Report combined testing rates at the joint TB/substance misuse governance meeting to keep the pathway prioritised after staff turnover.
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from the substance misuse and TB screening records
pass: For a person under 65 in regular contact with prison substance misuse services (at an establishment receiving prisoners from high-incidence areas), the record shows an interferon-gamma release assay for TB was offered at the same time as hepatitis B/C and HIV testing.

question: What proportion of prisoners in prison for the first time are screened for TB within 48 hours of arrival?
why: TB screening within 48 hours of arrival is a specific, time-critical NG57 standard distinct from the first- and second-stage general health assessments, and is easy to lose track of separately if not tracked as its own metric. No audit in corpus of the 48-hour TB screening timescale specifically has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG57 Physical health of people in prison, rec 1.1.9 (2016), adapted from the NICE guideline on tuberculosis
standard.wording: Healthcare professionals in prisons should ensure people coming into prison are screened for TB within 48 hours of arrival.

population: All new receptions over the audit period. Exclude same-day transfers from another prison with a documented TB screen completed there within the last 48 hours.
sample: 40 consecutive new receptions over the last 4 weeks.
data_source: Prison electronic health record, TB screening register, reception log.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic 'TB screen due within 48 hours' countdown task to the reception worklist, visible to the nursing team separately from the general first/second-stage assessment tasks.
reaudit: At 3 months, same reception log and template.
close_loop: Present to the local multidisciplinary TB team and prison health governance board; if the separate countdown task works, keep it as a standing item on the reception dashboard.
evidence: No audit in corpus of TB screening completion within the specific 48-hour NG57 timescale.
pitfalls: TB screening may be recorded as part of the general health assessment without a separate timestamp → add a dedicated TB screening field with its own date/time.
Access to mobile X-ray or IGRA testing may be limited out of hours → agree local arrangements for weekend and night receptions before cycle 1.
People who decline screening should be recorded distinctly from those simply not yet screened → add a 'declined' option to avoid conflating the two.
High reception volumes on a single day can delay screening for later arrivals → review results by daily reception volume.
Improvement may fade if the countdown task is not maintained after an IT upgrade → confirm the task list still functions at re-audit.
pearls: Recruit the reception nurse lead and the local multidisciplinary TB team liaison together.
Agree out-of-hours screening arrangements (for example, symptom screen with X-ray to follow) before cycle 1.
Use the same reception log extraction method at re-audit.
Report the 48-hour completion rate at the multidisciplinary TB team meeting so it remains visible after the audit lead moves on.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the prison health record
pass: TB screening (symptom screen, and chest X-ray or IGRA as locally protocolised) is documented as completed within 48 hours of the recorded reception date and time.

question: When an ACCT is opened for a prisoner, what proportion of first case reviews have healthcare or mental health staff attendance, or a documented written/verbal contribution, recorded?
why: Health input at the first ACCT case review is intended to bring clinical information into the multi-disciplinary safety planning for prisoners at risk of self-harm or suicide, but attendance is not automatic and depends on healthcare being invited and available. No audit in corpus of healthcare attendance or contribution at first ACCT case reviews has been published in the library.

standard.source: Prison Safety Policy Framework, paragraph 4.184 (re-issued 14 January 2026)
standard.wording: Healthcare or mental health staff must attend the first case review. If in exceptional circumstances they cannot attend, a verbal or written contribution must be provided. A further ACCT case review must then be convened as soon as possible.

population: All ACCT documents opened in the establishment over the audit period. Exclude ACCTs closed before a first case review could take place (for example, same-day resolution).
sample: 40 consecutive ACCT openings over the last 3 months, or all if fewer.
data_source: ACCT case review records, prison electronic health record cross-referenced with NOMIS ACCT alerts.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic healthcare notification when a concern form is raised (as required by paragraph 4.173/4.184), with the first case review time only confirmed once healthcare has acknowledged attendance or provided a contribution.
reaudit: At 3 months, same ACCT case review records and template.
close_loop: Present at the joint safer custody and healthcare governance meeting; if the notification-and-acknowledgement step works, embed it as the establishment's standard ACCT healthcare pathway.
evidence: No audit in corpus of healthcare attendance or contribution at first ACCT case reviews.
pitfalls: Healthcare staffing levels may not allow attendance at every case review, especially out of hours → ensure the written/verbal contribution route is genuinely available as a fallback.
'Attendance' may be recorded loosely without confirming a genuine clinical contribution was made → audit the content of the contribution, not just a tick box.
ACCT and healthcare records sit on different IT systems in most establishments → agree a cross-referencing method before cycle 1.
Case reviews may be rescheduled at short notice, making healthcare attendance harder to plan → build early notification into the concern-form process, as the framework requires.
Improvement may fade if the notification step is seen as an add-on rather than mandatory → make it part of the ACCT case co-ordinator's checklist.
pearls: Recruit the safer custody lead and the prison's senior healthcare clinical lead jointly, since this crosses both services.
Agree the notification and escalation process with both teams before cycle 1.
Use the same ACCT/case review extraction method at re-audit.
Report results at the joint safer custody and healthcare governance meeting so the pathway survives staff turnover.
effort: ~20 min per 10 ACCT case reviews from ACCT and health records
pass: The first ACCT case review record shows healthcare or mental health staff attended in person, or a documented written or verbal contribution from healthcare was provided if they could not attend.

question: What proportion of people discharged or transferred from prison with an ongoing prescription are given at least 7 days of their prescribed medicines or an FP10 prescription?
why: A gap in medicines supply at the point of release or transfer is a recognised risk for relapse, overdose and loss of continuity of care, and depends on planning that can be missed with short-notice releases. No audit in corpus of the 7-day discharge medicines supply standard has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG57 Physical health of people in prison, rec 1.7.14 (2016)
standard.wording: When a person is discharged or transferred from prison, give them a minimum of 7 days' prescribed medicines or an FP10 prescription, based on a risk assessment.

population: All people discharged (released to the community, not transferred between custodial settings) from the prison with at least one ongoing prescribed medicine, over the audit period. Exclude people with no ongoing prescription at release.
sample: 40 consecutive releases with an ongoing prescription over the last 4 weeks.
data_source: Prison electronic health record, discharge medicines record, pharmacy dispensing log.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'discharge medicines: days supplied' field to the release checklist that must show 7 or more (or a linked risk assessment) before the release paperwork can be signed off by pharmacy.
reaudit: At 3 months, same discharge records and template.
close_loop: Present at the medicines optimisation and resettlement governance meeting; if the mandatory field works, keep it as a standard release checklist item.
evidence: No audit in corpus of the 7-day discharge medicines supply standard on release from prison.
pitfalls: Short-notice releases (for example, following a court decision) leave little time to prepare medicines → build a same-day pharmacy fast-track process for unplanned releases (see NG57 1.7.15).
Controlled drugs and opioid substitution therapy need specific arrangements with community providers → confirm the community pharmacy handover process before cycle 1.
People released without a fixed address may struggle to access a community pharmacy → note this in the risk assessment rather than skipping the medicines supply.
FP10 prescriptions may not be dispensed promptly in the community → measure days supplied given directly where possible, not just the prescription being issued.
Improvement may fade if pharmacy staffing is reduced → review staffing alongside the audit results.
pearls: Recruit the prison pharmacist and resettlement/throughcare team jointly.
Agree the fast-track process for unplanned releases before cycle 1, as NG57 requires a contingency plan.
Use the same discharge record extraction method at re-audit.
Report results at the resettlement and medicines optimisation governance meetings so the checklist item survives contract or staff changes.
effort: ~15 min per 10 discharges from the prison health record and pharmacy log
pass: The discharge/transfer record shows the person was given at least 7 days' supply of each ongoing prescribed medicine, or an FP10 prescription covering at least 7 days, unless a documented risk assessment specifies a different amount.

question: What proportion of people in prison who smoke are offered stop-smoking support at their first-stage health assessment, in a smoke-free establishment?
why: Prisons in England and Wales are smoke-free, and reception is a key opportunity to offer stop-smoking or nicotine replacement support to a population with a much higher smoking prevalence than the general community, but this can be overshadowed by the many other items covered at reception. No audit in corpus of stop-smoking support offered at prison reception has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG209 Tobacco: preventing uptake, promoting quitting and treating dependence, rec 1.12.1 and 1.12.2 (2021, amended 2025)
standard.wording: Tell people who smoke that a range of interventions is available to help them stop smoking. Explain how to access them and refer people to stop-smoking support if appropriate... Ensure the following are accessible to adults who smoke: behavioural interventions... nicotine replacement therapy (NRT).

population: All new receptions over the audit period who report current smoking at first-stage assessment. Exclude non-smokers and long-term vapers only.
sample: 40 consecutive receptions reporting current smoking over the last 4 weeks.
data_source: Prison electronic health record, first-stage assessment template, NRT prescribing record.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'smoker: NRT/stop-smoking support offered' field to the first-stage reception template, linked directly to an NRT prescribing order set so support can be started the same day.
reaudit: At 3 months, same reception log and template.
close_loop: Present to the prison health and justice governance board; if the mandatory field and linked order set work, embed them as the standard smoke-free reception pathway.
evidence: No audit in corpus of stop-smoking support offered at prison reception.
pitfalls: Reception staff have many competing priorities at first-stage assessment → make the smoking field mandatory rather than optional to prevent it being missed.
Withdrawal symptoms may be attributed to other causes if not specifically asked about → train reception staff to recognise and act on nicotine withdrawal.
NRT stock shortages can undermine same-day support → confirm supply arrangements with pharmacy before cycle 1.
Vaping status may not be captured separately from smoking, complicating the denominator → clarify the definition of 'current smoker' before starting.
Improvement may fade if NRT is only offered at reception and not continued on the wing → check continuation rates as a secondary measure.
pearls: Recruit the reception nurse lead and the prison's smoke-free/stop-smoking coordinator jointly.
Agree the NRT order set and supply arrangements with pharmacy before cycle 1.
Use the same reception log extraction method at re-audit.
Report results at the smoke-free prison steering group to keep the pathway prioritised after staff turnover.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the prison health record
pass: The first-stage health assessment record shows smoking status was asked, and, for a current smoker, that stop-smoking support (behavioural support and/or NRT) was offered before or at the point of reception into the smoke-free establishment.

question: What proportion of adults with hypertension aged under 80 on antihypertensive treatment have a clinic blood pressure below 140/90 mmHg at their most recent reading?
why: Blood pressure treatment to target is one of the largest levers for preventing stroke and cardiovascular events in general practice, but achievement of the specific NICE target (as opposed to diagnosis or QOF recording) is not routinely closed-loop audited. No closed-loop audit in corpus targets the NG136 clinic BP treatment target for adults under 80.

standard.source: NICE NG136 Hypertension in adults: diagnosis and management, rec 1.4.20 (2019, amended 2022)
standard.wording: For adults with hypertension aged under 80, reduce clinic blood pressure to below 140/90 mmHg and ensure that it is maintained below that level.

population: Adults aged 18 to 79 on the practice hypertension register, on one or more antihypertensive medicines for at least 3 months, with a clinic BP reading in the last 12 months. Exclude patients using home or ambulatory targets only, or with white-coat/masked hypertension under active review.
sample: 40 consecutive patients from the hypertension register meeting the inclusion criteria, or a 10% random sample if the register is larger.
data_source: Practice hypertension register, GP clinical system BP readings, repeat prescription record.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Run a monthly practice search flagging hypertension register patients whose last clinic BP is above target with no medication change or clinic BP recheck in the last 8 weeks, for pharmacist-led review.
reaudit: At 6 months, same register and template.
close_loop: Present at the practice's QOF/long-term conditions meeting; if the monthly search improves target achievement, add it to the pharmacist's standing task list.
evidence: No closed-loop audit in corpus of NG136 clinic blood pressure target achievement in adults under 80.
pitfalls: A single high reading may not reflect true control → use the most recent recorded reading but flag patients for a re-check rather than assuming poor control from one value.
White-coat effect can make clinic readings appear worse than home readings → review NG136's advice on ABPM/HBPM for patients with a suspected white-coat effect.
Medication non-adherence is a common but under-recorded reason for poor control → include an adherence check in the pharmacist review.
Frailty and multimorbidity may justify a less strict target in practice, even under 80 → document clinical judgement clearly rather than treating every above-target reading as a failure.
Improvement may fade if the monthly search is not resourced → confirm pharmacist time is protected before cycle 1.
pearls: Recruit the practice's clinical pharmacist to lead the medication reviews generated by the search.
Agree the exclusion criteria (diabetes/severe CKD targets, white-coat effect) with the GP lead before cycle 1.
Use the same register extraction method at re-audit for a fair comparison.
Report target-achievement rates at the practice's QOF preparation meeting to keep this visible year-round, not just at year-end.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the hypertension register and BP readings
pass: The most recent clinic blood pressure reading in the last 12 months is below 140/90 mmHg. For patients with type 1 diabetes or severe chronic kidney disease, use the NG136 table 1 target for that condition instead.

question: What proportion of adults with atrial fibrillation and a CHA2DS2-VASc score of 2 or more are prescribed a direct-acting oral anticoagulant or warfarin?
why: Undertreatment of stroke risk in atrial fibrillation remains a major preventable cause of stroke, and while CHA2DS2-VASc scoring is often recorded, whether anticoagulation is actually prescribed for those who meet the threshold is less often specifically audited in primary care. No closed-loop primary care audit in corpus targets anticoagulation prescribing against the CHA2DS2-VASc threshold itself (as opposed to scoring completion or single-drug-class checks).

standard.source: NICE NG196 Atrial fibrillation: diagnosis and management, rec 1.6.3 (2021)
standard.wording: Offer anticoagulation with a direct-acting oral anticoagulant to people with atrial fibrillation and a CHA2DS2-VASc score of 2 or above, taking into account the risk of bleeding.

population: Adults on the practice atrial fibrillation register with a documented CHA2DS2-VASc score of 2 or more. Exclude patients with a score of 0-1 (where anticoagulation is not routinely recommended) and patients already excluded from anticoagulation for a valve-related indication requiring warfarin-specific pathways if being separately managed by a specialist.
sample: 40 consecutive patients from the AF register with CHA2DS2-VASc ≥2, or a 10% random sample if the register is larger.
data_source: Practice AF register, CHA2DS2-VASc coded score, repeat prescription record.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Run a monthly practice search cross-referencing the AF register, CHA2DS2-VASc score and current anticoagulant prescription, generating a task for GP review of every patient scoring ≥2 with no anticoagulant and no documented reason.
reaudit: At 6 months, same register and template.
close_loop: Present at the practice's QOF/long-term conditions meeting; if the monthly search closes the gap, add it to the standing list of chronic disease searches.
evidence: No closed-loop primary care audit in corpus of anticoagulation prescribing against the CHA2DS2-VASc ≥2 threshold.
pitfalls: CHA2DS2-VASc scores may be out of date if not recalculated after a new diagnosis (for example, new diabetes or heart failure) → recalculate at the point of audit, not just use the last coded score.
Patients may be correctly excluded for a specific contraindication (for example, active bleeding) → always check for a documented reason before counting as a gap.
Some patients may be under specialist anticoagulation clinics with prescribing outside the GP record → check shared care records before concluding a patient is untreated.
Patient choice to decline anticoagulation after full discussion is a valid outcome → record this distinctly from an unexplained gap.
Improvement may fade if the search is run once and not repeated → make it a standing monthly search, not a one-off audit tool.
pearls: Recruit the practice's cardiovascular disease lead GP or pharmacist to review flagged patients.
Agree the exclusion criteria (score, contraindications, specialist care) with the whole team before cycle 1.
Use the same register extraction method at re-audit for a fair comparison.
Report the gap-closure rate at the QOF preparation meeting to keep this visible after the audit lead moves on.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the AF register and prescribing record
pass: The patient is prescribed a DOAC or warfarin, or has a clearly documented reason for not being anticoagulated (for example, a specific contraindication or a fully informed decision to decline after discussion of risks and benefits).

question: What proportion of adults with one of the NICE risk factors for chronic kidney disease (diabetes, hypertension, cardiovascular disease or previous acute kidney injury) have had both an eGFR and a urine albumin:creatinine ratio (ACR) tested in the last 12 months?
why: ACR testing is frequently omitted even when eGFR is checked, meaning early CKD with normal eGFR but raised ACR (which independently predicts adverse outcomes) is missed. No closed-loop audit in corpus specifically targets ACR testing coverage in at-risk groups alongside eGFR.

standard.source: NICE NG203 Chronic kidney disease: assessment and management, rec 1.1.21 (2021)
standard.wording: Offer testing for CKD using eGFRcreatinine and ACR to adults with any of the following risk factors: diabetes; hypertension; previous episode of acute kidney injury; cardiovascular disease (ischaemic heart disease, chronic heart failure, peripheral vascular disease or cerebral vascular disease); structural renal tract disease, recurrent renal calculi or prostatic hypertrophy; multisystem diseases with potential kidney involvement... gout; family history of end-stage renal disease... or hereditary kidney disease; incidental detection of haematuria or proteinuria.

population: Adults on the practice's diabetes, hypertension or cardiovascular disease registers (or coded with a previous acute kidney injury episode) without a diagnosis of CKD already established at stage G3a or above with a recorded ACR. Exclude patients under active nephrology follow-up with their own testing schedule.
sample: 40 consecutive patients from the combined at-risk registers, or a 10% random sample if larger.
data_source: Diabetes/hypertension/CVD registers, laboratory results (eGFR and ACR), GP clinical system.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add ACR to the default annual review blood test order set for diabetes, hypertension and cardiovascular disease reviews, so it is requested automatically alongside eGFR rather than as a separate step.
reaudit: At 6 months, same registers and template.
close_loop: Present at the practice's QOF/long-term conditions meeting; if the combined order set improves ACR testing, keep it as the default for all relevant annual reviews.
evidence: No closed-loop audit in corpus of ACR testing coverage alongside eGFR in NICE-defined CKD risk groups.
pitfalls: ACR requires a urine sample that patients may not bring to the same appointment as blood tests → provide a sample pot and instructions in advance of the review, or a postal kit if available.
