Some laboratories process ACR separately from routine biochemistry, causing results to be missed on a quick chart review → confirm the exact test code used locally before starting.
Patients already diagnosed with advanced CKD under nephrology may have testing arranged elsewhere → exclude them or verify with the specialist team.
A raised ACR needs a repeat confirmatory test before diagnosis → make this clear in staff training so a single result is interpreted correctly.
Improvement may fade if the order set is reverted during an EPR template update → check it remains in place at re-audit.
pearls: Recruit the practice's diabetes or CKD lead nurse to champion the combined order set.
Agree the exact local ACR test code and sample logistics with the laboratory before cycle 1.
Use the same register definitions at re-audit for a fair comparison.
Report ACR testing rates at QOF preparation meetings to keep this visible after the lead rotates.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the registers and laboratory results
pass: Both an eGFR and a urine ACR result are recorded in the last 12 months for a patient with one or more of the listed NICE risk factors.

question: What proportion of adults and children aged 5 and over on the practice asthma register have a documented, reviewed personalised asthma action plan?
why: A written personalised action plan halves the risk of hospital admission for asthma, but plan issue and subsequent review at key points (admission, acute consultation, annual review) are inconsistently tracked as a single closed-loop measure. No closed-loop audit in corpus specifically targets the presence and review of a personalised asthma action plan under the current joint BTS/NICE/SIGN guideline.

standard.source: NICE NG245 Asthma: diagnosis, monitoring and management (BTS/NICE/SIGN), rec 1.14.1 and 1.14.2 (2024)
standard.wording: For adults, young people and children aged 5 and over with a diagnosis of asthma... offer an asthma self-management programme, comprising a documented personalised action plan and education... Review the content of the personalised action plan, and check that the person understands it, at the following: hospital admission, including in virtual wards; acute consultations in primary care or emergency department; annual reviews.

population: Patients aged 5 and over on the practice asthma register with an annual review, acute asthma consultation, or hospital admission in the last 12 months. Exclude patients with asthma in remission and no contact in the last 12 months.
sample: 40 consecutive patients from the asthma register with a qualifying contact in the last 12 months, or a 10% random sample if larger.
data_source: Asthma register, GP clinical template for asthma review, hospital discharge letters.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'action plan issued/reviewed' field to the asthma annual review and acute asthma consultation templates, which cannot be closed until completed, with a printable or app-based plan generated automatically.
reaudit: At 6 months, same register and template.
close_loop: Present at the practice's respiratory/QOF meeting; if the mandatory field works, keep it in all three trigger-point templates (annual review, acute consultation, admission follow-up) permanently.
evidence: No closed-loop audit in corpus of personalised asthma action plan issue and review under NG245.
pitfalls: A plan may be issued once and never reviewed again, appearing compliant on a simple 'exists' check → audit review at the most recent qualifying contact, not just existence.
Post-hospital-admission plans may be created by the hospital but not visible in the GP record → request a copy be sent with every discharge letter.
Children under 5 are excluded from the mandatory plan (self-management programmes for carers instead) → apply the correct age threshold in the template.
Time pressure in 10-minute appointments can squeeze out plan review → protect specific time in asthma review templates for this step.
Improvement may fade if the mandatory field becomes a routine tick without real review → spot-check free text for genuine discussion at re-audit.
pearls: Recruit the practice's respiratory/asthma lead nurse to champion the mandatory template field.
Agree a standard action plan format (paper or app-based) with the team before cycle 1.
Use the same register and qualifying-contact definitions at re-audit for a fair comparison.
Report plan review rates at the respiratory/QOF meeting to keep this visible after the lead rotates.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the asthma register and consultation templates
pass: A documented personalised asthma action plan exists in the record and has been reviewed (content checked and understanding confirmed) at the most recent annual review, acute consultation, or hospital admission, whichever was most recent.

question: What proportion of adults admitted with a COPD exacerbation in the last year who remain at risk of exacerbations have a documented individualised exacerbation action plan, with a short course of oral corticosteroids and antibiotics to keep at home?
why: Rescue packs are widely prescribed but a formal, individualised exacerbation action plan explaining when and how to use them, and how to get replacements, is a distinct and less consistently documented step. No closed-loop audit in corpus specifically targets the combination of exacerbation action plan plus rescue pack issue under NG115.

standard.source: NICE NG115 Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in over 16s, rec 1.2.128 (2018)
standard.wording: Offer people a short course of oral corticosteroids and a short course of oral antibiotics to keep at home as part of their exacerbation action plan if: they have had an exacerbation within the last year, and remain at risk of exacerbations; they understand and are confident about when and how to take these medicines, and the associated benefits and harms; they know to tell their healthcare professional when they have used the medicines, and to ask for replacements.

population: Adults on the COPD register who had an exacerbation (primary care treated or hospital admission) in the last 12 months and remain at risk of further exacerbations (previous frequent exacerbator or ongoing risk factors). Exclude patients with a documented reason a rescue pack is unsuitable (for example, cognitive impairment without a carer able to manage it safely).
sample: 40 consecutive patients on the COPD register with an exacerbation in the last 12 months, or a 10% random sample if larger.
data_source: COPD register, GP consultation and review templates, repeat prescription record for rescue pack medicines.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'exacerbation action plan and rescue pack' section to the COPD annual review and post-exacerbation follow-up templates, generating a printed plan and linked repeat prescription automatically.
reaudit: At 6 months, same register and template.
close_loop: Present at the practice's respiratory/QOF meeting; if the mandatory section improves documented plan issue, keep it in the standard COPD review and post-exacerbation pathway.
evidence: No closed-loop audit in corpus of the combined exacerbation action plan and rescue pack standard under NG115.
pitfalls: Rescue packs may be repeatedly issued without ever reviewing whether the patient understands how to use them safely → audit understanding confirmation, not just supply.
Patients using 3 or more courses in a year need specific review of possible reasons, per NG115 1.2.130 → flag these patients for a dedicated consultation rather than automatic re-issue.
Self-management may not suit patients with cognitive impairment living alone → document a clear individual risk assessment rather than a blanket policy.
Rescue pack medicines can be stockpiled or used inappropriately if not reviewed → check medicine cupboard content at annual review where practical.
Improvement may fade if the mandatory template section is skipped under time pressure → protect appointment time for COPD reviews.
pearls: Recruit the practice's respiratory lead nurse to champion the mandatory template section.
Agree the exact rescue pack medicines and quantities with the GP lead before cycle 1.
Use the same register and exacerbation definitions at re-audit for a fair comparison.
Report over-use flags (3+ courses) at the respiratory/QOF meeting to sustain the review pathway after staff rotate.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the COPD register and review templates
pass: A documented, individualised exacerbation action plan is in the record, a rescue pack (oral corticosteroid and antibiotic) has been supplied to keep at home, and the record shows the patient was told to inform the practice when used and to request replacements.

question: What proportion of patients on shared-care methotrexate monitoring in general practice have had FBC, liver function tests and renal function checked within the interval specified in the shared care protocol?
why: Methotrexate monitoring is delegated to general practice under shared care agreements, but responsibility for chasing results and acting on abnormal or overdue tests can fall between the specialist and GP practice. No closed-loop audit in corpus specifically targets adherence to the agreed monitoring interval for shared-care DMARDs in general practice.

standard.source: NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service, Methotrexate monitoring (based on British Society for Rheumatology shared care guidance)
standard.wording: Every 2-3 months: Full blood count; Liver function tests; Serum creatinine (for creatinine clearance) or Estimated glomerular filtration rate. [Rheumatology and gastroenterology, once stable]: At least every 12 weeks: Full blood count; Liver function tests; Serum creatinine.

population: Patients on the practice's DMARD/methotrexate shared care register, on a stable dose for at least 3 months. Exclude patients recently started or with a dose change in the last 6 weeks, who need more frequent monitoring under a different part of the protocol.
sample: 40 consecutive patients on the shared care methotrexate register, or all if fewer.
data_source: Practice DMARD/shared care register, laboratory results, shared care agreement documentation.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Run a monthly practice search identifying shared-care methotrexate patients overdue their monitoring interval, generating an automatic recall to the patient and a task to the practice pharmacist.
reaudit: At 6 months, same register and template.
close_loop: Present at the practice's medicines optimisation/QOF meeting; if the monthly search closes the gap, add it to the standing list of shared-care searches run alongside other DMARD safety checks.
evidence: No closed-loop audit in corpus of shared-care methotrexate monitoring interval adherence in general practice.
pitfalls: Monitoring intervals vary between individual shared care protocols and specialties → record the specific agreed interval for each patient rather than assuming one national standard.
Results may be filed without being reviewed against the expected interval → build an interval check into the search, not just a search for any recent bloods.
Patients who do not attend for monitoring bloods may have their methotrexate wrongly continued → build in a rule to flag and consider withholding the prescription if overdue.
Shared care responsibilities may be unclear between specialist and GP, especially soon after a hospital discharge → confirm and document the shared care agreement for every patient.
Improvement may fade if the pharmacist task list is not resourced → confirm protected time before cycle 1.
pearls: Recruit the practice's clinical pharmacist to lead the monthly monitoring search, since they already manage repeat prescribing safety.
Agree the individual monitoring interval for each patient with the specialist shared care letter before cycle 1.
Use the same register and interval definitions at re-audit for a fair comparison.
Report overdue-monitoring rates at the medicines optimisation meeting to sustain the pathway after staff rotate.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the DMARD register and laboratory results
pass: FBC, LFTs and renal function (creatinine or eGFR) are all recorded within the interval specified in the patient's individual shared care protocol (no more than 12 weeks for stable patients on rheumatology/gastroenterology shared care, or as otherwise specified).

question: What proportion of people prescribed systemic HRT for menopausal symptoms have a documented review at 3 months of starting or changing treatment?
why: The 3-month review is when efficacy, tolerability and expected side effects such as unscheduled bleeding are checked, but it is easy for repeat prescribing to continue without a structured review taking place. No closed-loop audit in corpus specifically targets completion of the NG23 3-month HRT review.

standard.source: NICE NG23 Menopause: diagnosis and management, rec 1.9.2 (2015)
standard.wording: Review each treatment for symptoms associated with menopause: at 3 months to assess efficacy and tolerability; annually thereafter, unless there are clinical indications for an earlier review (such as treatment ineffectiveness, side effects or adverse events).

population: Patients who started HRT for the first time, or had a dose or preparation change, in the last 6 months, allowing time to have reached the 3-month review window. Exclude patients who stopped HRT before 3 months for an unrelated reason.
sample: 40 consecutive patients starting or changing HRT over the last 6 months, or all if fewer.
data_source: Repeat prescription record (start/change dates), GP consultation templates, menopause review template.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic 3-month HRT review task to the practice system, generated whenever a new HRT prescription or dose/preparation change is issued, with a structured review template pre-populated with the bleeding-pattern question.
reaudit: At 6 months, same prescribing record and template.
close_loop: Present at the practice's women's health/QOF meeting; if the automatic task works, keep it live for every new HRT start or change.
evidence: No closed-loop audit in corpus of HRT 3-month review completion under NG23.
pitfalls: Repeat HRT prescriptions can be issued by reception or pharmacy without a clinician review being triggered → build the review task into the prescribing system itself, not rely on staff memory.
Reviews may happen but not be coded as such, undercounting true compliance → agree a specific template or code for the 3-month review before cycle 1.
Telephone or online reviews may be harder to capture consistently than face-to-face → include all consultation modes in the audit definition.
Patients may not attend the review appointment → record non-attendance and re-invitation separately from a failure to offer.
Improvement may fade if the automatic task is switched off during a system update → confirm it remains active at re-audit.
pearls: Recruit the practice's menopause or women's health lead GP or nurse to champion the automatic task.
Agree the review template content (efficacy, tolerability, bleeding pattern) with the team before cycle 1.
Use the same prescribing record extraction method at re-audit for a fair comparison.
Report review completion rates at the women's health/QOF meeting to sustain the pathway after the lead rotates.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the prescribing record and consultation templates
pass: A documented review (efficacy, tolerability, and, for patients with a uterus, discussion of expected bleeding patterns) is recorded within 3 months (10-16 weeks) of starting HRT or changing the dose or preparation.

question: What proportion of adult patients with a new safeguarding concern raised in a GP consultation have that concern coded in their electronic record using the practice's agreed safeguarding code?
why: Safeguarding concerns raised in consultations are sometimes documented only in free text, which is not searchable for multi-agency information sharing, case conferences or future risk assessment. No audit in corpus specifically targets the coding (as opposed to the existence) of adult or child safeguarding concerns in the GP record.

standard.source: Local standard, informed by RCGP safeguarding recording principles and NHS England information-sharing requirements for safeguarding
standard.wording: A safeguarding concern raised in a consultation should be recorded using a specific, searchable safeguarding code in the patient's electronic record, in addition to any free-text description, so that the concern can be identified for information sharing, multi-agency working and future risk assessment.

population: All adult and child consultations over the audit period where a safeguarding concern is mentioned in the free-text notes. Exclude routine safeguarding training or administrative entries with no individual patient concern.
sample: 40 consecutive consultations with a free-text safeguarding concern identified by a text search over the last 3 months, or all if fewer.
data_source: GP consultation free-text search, coded record entries, safeguarding register.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a pop-up prompt in the EPR whenever certain safeguarding-related free-text phrases are entered, asking the clinician to confirm and apply the specific safeguarding code before the consultation can be saved.
reaudit: At 3 months, same free-text search and template.
close_loop: Present at the practice's safeguarding lead meeting; if the pop-up prompt improves coding, keep it live and review the trigger phrase list periodically with the safeguarding lead.
evidence: No audit in corpus of safeguarding concern coding completeness in general practice records.
pitfalls: A free-text search will miss concerns described in varied language → use a broad set of trigger phrases and accept the search will not be exhaustive.
Coding a safeguarding concern raises confidentiality and information-governance questions → confirm the practice's information-sharing policy with the safeguarding lead before cycle 1.
Clinicians may worry that coding could affect the patient relationship if seen by the patient online → clarify with the safeguarding lead what is and is not visible to patients via online access.
Over-triggering the pop-up prompt on unrelated entries could cause alert fatigue → refine the trigger phrase list after an initial pilot.
Improvement may fade if the pop-up is disabled during an EPR update → confirm it is still active at re-audit.
pearls: Recruit the practice's named safeguarding lead GP or nurse to define the trigger phrases and code.
Agree the information-governance approach with the safeguarding lead and practice manager before cycle 1.
Use the same free-text search terms at re-audit for a fair comparison.
Report coding completeness at the practice's safeguarding supervision meetings to keep this prioritised after the lead changes.
effort: ~20 min per 10 consultations from the free-text search and coded record
pass: A new safeguarding concern documented in the consultation free text is also recorded using the practice's specific safeguarding code (for example, 'safeguarding adult concern' or 'safeguarding child concern') within the same working day.

question: What proportion of adults aged 6 months to 64 years in a clinical risk group for influenza are on the practice's flu register and are invited for vaccination each season?
why: Uptake of flu vaccine in at-risk adults under 65 is persistently lower than in the over-65 routine cohort, and depends on the practice proactively compiling and using a risk-group register rather than waiting for patients to request vaccination. No closed-loop audit in corpus targets flu register completeness for under-65 at-risk adults specifically.

standard.source: UKHSA Green Book, Influenza chapter (25 August 2026)
standard.wording: General practitioners are required to proactively identify all those for whom influenza immunisations are indicated and to compile a register of those patients for whom influenza immunisation is recommended. Sufficient vaccine can then be ordered in advance and patients can be invited to planned immunisation sessions or appointments.

population: Patients aged 6 months to 64 years with a coded qualifying clinical risk group, active on the practice list at the start of the flu season. Exclude patients already vaccinated elsewhere (for example, by a community pharmacy) with evidence in the record.
sample: 40 consecutive patients from the combined risk-group registers, or a 10% random sample if larger.
data_source: Practice clinical risk registers (respiratory, cardiac, diabetes, renal, liver, immunosuppression), flu vaccination call/recall log.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Build a single combined flu risk-group search that pulls from all individual chronic disease registers automatically each August, generating the season's invitation list without relying on manual compilation.
reaudit: At the start of the next flu season, same combined search and template.
close_loop: Present at the practice's flu campaign planning meeting; if the combined search improves register completeness, keep it as the default pre-season process.
evidence: No closed-loop audit in corpus of flu register completeness for under-65 at-risk adults.
pitfalls: Risk-group coding is inconsistent between clinicians, so some eligible patients may not appear on any register → review and standardise the code list with the coding lead before the season starts.
Patients newly diagnosed with a risk factor after the initial register is built may be missed → re-run the search monthly through the season, not just once in August.
Vaccination given outside the practice (community pharmacy, hospital) may not be recorded in the GP system → check the national vaccination record where available.
Vaccine supply constraints can affect invitation timing → report supply issues separately from register or invitation failures.
Improvement may fade if the combined search is not re-run every season → build it into the annual flu campaign checklist.
pearls: Recruit the practice's flu campaign lead nurse to own the combined register search.
Agree the risk-group code list with the whole clinical team before the season starts.
Use the same combined search method at re-audit for a fair comparison.
Review register completeness at the practice's pre-season flu planning meeting each year so it is not forgotten after staff turnover.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the combined risk registers and flu call/recall log
pass: A patient with a coded clinical risk group qualifying for flu vaccination (chronic respiratory, heart, kidney or liver disease, diabetes, immunosuppression, or other Green Book risk group) aged 6 months to 64 years is included on the practice's flu register and has a documented invitation for the current season.

question: What proportion of adults aged 65 and over on the practice list have a record of having received a pneumococcal vaccine (PPV23 or PCV20)?
why: Pneumococcal vaccination at 65 is a single, once-only dose that is easy to miss for patients who turned 65 before electronic call/recall systems were fully established, or who registered later in life, and coverage in this whole-population cohort is rarely audited as its own measure. No closed-loop audit in corpus targets pneumococcal vaccination coverage in the whole 65-and-over population.

standard.source: UKHSA Green Book, Pneumococcal chapter (29 July 2026)
standard.wording: Adults aged 65 years and over, and clinical risk groups aged 2 years or over: a single dose of 0.5ml of PPV23 or PCV20.

population: All patients aged 65 and over registered with the practice for at least 12 months. Exclude patients who have already received PPV23/PCV20 in a clinical risk group before age 65.
sample: 40 consecutive patients aged 65 and over identified by a practice search, or a 10% random sample if the cohort is larger.
data_source: Practice age-based population search, immunisation record.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Run a one-off practice-wide search of all patients aged 65 and over with no recorded pneumococcal vaccine, and add a standing rule that the vaccine is offered automatically at the 65th birthday alongside the shingles vaccination invitation.
reaudit: At 6 months, same age-based search and template.
close_loop: Present at the practice's immunisation/QOF meeting; if the standing 65th-birthday rule improves coverage, keep it running permanently alongside the shingles invitation.
evidence: No closed-loop audit in corpus of whole-population pneumococcal vaccination coverage in adults aged 65 and over.
pitfalls: Historic paper records may not have been fully migrated to the electronic system → check paper records for older patients before concluding a vaccine was never given.
Patients vaccinated by a previous practice may not have the record transferred → request records from PCSE/previous practice where the immunisation history is unclear.
Combining the invitation with the shingles vaccination call reduces extra appointments but requires coordination → agree the combined invitation letter wording before cycle 1.
Small numbers of long-standing gaps may reflect genuine past declines → record a documented decline separately from a true gap in offering.
Improvement may fade if the 65th-birthday rule is not maintained after an EPR template change → confirm it is still active at re-audit.
pearls: Recruit the practice's immunisation lead nurse to run the age-based search and design the combined invitation.
Agree the combined pneumococcal/shingles invitation letter with the practice manager before cycle 1.
Use the same age-based search definitions at re-audit for a fair comparison.
Report coverage rates at the immunisation/QOF meeting to keep the standing rule visible after the lead rotates.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the age-based search and immunisation record
pass: The patient's record shows a documented single dose of PPV23 or PCV20 given at or after age 65 (or in a qualifying risk group before 65, which satisfies the requirement without needing a repeat dose at 65).

question: What proportion of people transferring between prisons have relevant health record information (including current medicines) available to the receiving establishment's healthcare team before or at the point of transfer?
why: Loss of continuity of care and medicines information at inter-prison transfer is a recognised risk, particularly for people on complex regimens, opioid substitution therapy or mental health treatment. No audit in corpus of health information continuity specifically at inter-prison transfer has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG57 Physical health of people in prison, rec 1.7.3 (2016)
standard.wording: Ensure continuity of care between custodial settings, including court, the receiving prison or during escort periods by, for example: providing access to relevant information from the patient record; providing any medicines (including controlled drugs) - see also the section on continuity of medicines; issuing an FP10 prescription.

population: All people transferred between prisons (not first reception from the community or court) over the audit period. Exclude emergency hospital transfers, which are covered under a different pathway.
sample: 40 consecutive inter-prison transfers over the last 4 weeks, or all if fewer.
data_source: Prison electronic health record, prisoner escort record, medicine chart.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Introduce a standard transfer healthcare summary (including current medicines list) that must accompany every prisoner escort record electronically, checked as complete by the sending establishment's healthcare team before transfer.
reaudit: At 3 months, same transfer log and template.
close_loop: Present to the regional health and justice governance meeting, since this crosses establishments; if the standard summary works, embed it in the regional health and justice service specification.
evidence: No audit in corpus of health information continuity at inter-prison transfer.
pitfalls: Sending and receiving prisons may use different or non-linked IT systems → agree a minimum standard paper or electronic summary that works across systems.
Transfers can happen at short notice, leaving little time to prepare a full summary → build a rapid-summary template that can be completed quickly for urgent transfers.
Controlled drugs require additional security and documentation during transfer → confirm the local controlled drugs transfer protocol before cycle 1.
Escort staff may not prioritise healthcare paperwork among other transfer documents → make the health record a mandatory, checked item in the transfer process.
Improvement may fade without ongoing cross-establishment coordination → review the pathway with both establishments at re-audit, not just the sending one.
pearls: Recruit healthcare leads from both the sending and receiving establishments, since this audit spans two teams.
Agree a standard minimum data set for the transfer summary before cycle 1.
Use the same transfer log extraction method at re-audit for a fair comparison.
Report results at a regional (not just single-establishment) health and justice meeting so the pathway is adopted across multiple sites.
effort: ~15 min per 10 transfers from the prison health record and escort record
pass: At the point of arrival at the receiving prison, the healthcare team has access to relevant patient record information (including current medicines) from the sending establishment, and the person has been provided with sufficient medicines or an FP10 prescription to cover the transfer period without a missed dose.

question: What proportion of people entering prison who report drinking more than 15 units of alcohol daily, or who show signs of withdrawal, are urgently referred to the GP or an alternative healthcare professional at first-stage assessment?
why: Unrecognised or delayed management of alcohol withdrawal on reception into prison carries a risk of seizures and death, and depends on the first-stage screening question triggering an urgent, not routine, referral. No audit in corpus of urgent alcohol withdrawal referral timeliness at prison reception has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG57 Physical health of people in prison, rec 1.1.4 (table 1, item 13) (2016)
standard.wording: [Alcohol and substance misuse] Does the person drink alcohol, and if so: how much do they normally drink? how much did they drink in the week before coming into custody? Urgently refer the person to the GP or an alternative suitable healthcare professional if: they drink more than 15 units of alcohol daily or they are showing signs of withdrawal or they have been given medication for withdrawal in police or court cells.

population: All new receptions meeting one of the three urgent-referral criteria over the audit period. Exclude people already on an established prison alcohol withdrawal pathway from a very recent previous custodial episode with continuity of care already arranged.
sample: 40 consecutive receptions meeting the urgent-referral criteria over the last 6 weeks, or all if fewer.
data_source: First-stage assessment record, alcohol withdrawal (for example CIWA-Ar) monitoring chart, referral log.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Build an automatic same-shift alert to the on-call GP or clinical lead whenever the first-stage assessment template records one of the three urgent-referral criteria, with a linked withdrawal monitoring chart started at the same time.
reaudit: At 3 months, same reception records and template.
close_loop: Present to the prison substance misuse and safer custody governance meeting; if the automatic alert works, embed it as the standard reception alcohol pathway.
evidence: No audit in corpus of urgent alcohol withdrawal referral timeliness at prison reception.
pitfalls: Self-reported alcohol consumption may be under- or over-stated → use clinical judgement and any available third-party information (for example, police custody records) alongside self-report.
Withdrawal signs can develop hours after reception, after the first-stage assessment is complete → ensure ongoing monitoring is triggered, not just a one-off referral at reception.
Night or weekend receptions may have reduced on-call GP availability → confirm the out-of-hours escalation pathway before cycle 1.
Alcohol withdrawal management protocols vary between establishments → confirm the local monitoring chart and medication protocol with the clinical lead.
Improvement may fade if the automatic alert is disabled during an IT update → confirm it remains active at re-audit.
pearls: Recruit the prison's substance misuse lead clinician and reception nurse team jointly.
Agree the out-of-hours escalation pathway with the on-call GP rota before cycle 1.
Use the same urgent-referral criteria at re-audit for a fair comparison.
Report results at the substance misuse and safer custody governance meeting to sustain the pathway after staff turnover.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the reception record and withdrawal monitoring chart
pass: For a person reporting more than 15 units of alcohol daily, showing signs of withdrawal, or already given withdrawal medication in police or court cells, the record shows an urgent referral to the GP or an alternative suitable healthcare professional was made at, or immediately after, first-stage assessment (same shift).

question: What proportion of people in prison who score above threshold on the Correctional Mental Health Screen (CMHS-M or CMHS-W) at reception are referred for further mental health assessment?
why: The CMHS is a validated brief screen used to decide who needs further mental health assessment at reception, but a positive screen only reduces risk if it reliably leads to referral and assessment by a trained professional. No audit in corpus of referral completion after a positive CMHS score at prison reception has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG57 Physical health of people in prison, rec 1.1.17 (2016)
standard.wording: If there is other evidence supporting the likelihood of mental health problems, or a man scores 6 or more on the CMHS-M, or a woman scores 4 or more on the CMHS-W: a practitioner who is trained to perform an assessment of mental health problems should conduct further assessment or a practitioner who is not trained to perform an assessment of mental health problems should refer the person to an appropriately trained professional for further assessment.

population: All people screened with the CMHS-M or CMHS-W at reception over the audit period who scored above the referral threshold. Exclude people already under active mental health in-reach team follow-up at the time of screening.
sample: 40 consecutive above-threshold CMHS screens over the last 6 weeks, or all if fewer.
data_source: Prison electronic health record, CMHS screening tool record, mental health in-reach referral log.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic referral task to the mental health in-reach team's worklist whenever a CMHS score meets or exceeds the referral threshold, removing reliance on the reception clinician remembering to refer manually.
reaudit: At 3 months, same screening record and template.
close_loop: Present to the prison mental health in-reach governance meeting; if the automatic referral task works, embed it as the standard reception mental health pathway.
evidence: No audit in corpus of referral completion after a positive CMHS score at prison reception.
pitfalls: Reception staff may not always be trained to score the CMHS correctly → confirm scoring training is up to date before cycle 1.
Mental health in-reach team capacity may limit how quickly referrals can be seen → report waiting times as a secondary measure alongside referral completion.
Transgender patients require the CMHS version matching their gender identity, which staff may apply inconsistently → confirm staff know NG57's guidance on this before starting.
People who are unwilling or unable to engage with screening may be recorded as 'not screened' rather than a true negative → track these separately from below-threshold results.
Improvement may fade if the automatic referral task is not monitored → review the worklist regularly, not just at audit points.
pearls: Recruit the mental health in-reach team lead and reception nurse team jointly.
Agree the referral pathway and expected assessment timescale with the in-reach team before cycle 1.
Use the same CMHS threshold definitions at re-audit for a fair comparison.
Report referral and assessment completion rates at the mental health in-reach governance meeting to sustain the pathway after staff turnover.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the prison health record and referral log
pass: A person scoring 6 or more (men, CMHS-M) or 4 or more (women, CMHS-W) has a documented further mental health assessment, either conducted directly by a trained practitioner or via a referral to one, within 5 working days of the screen.

question: What proportion of people entering prison are offered hepatitis B vaccination at reception?
why: Hepatitis B vaccination on entry to prison protects a population at higher risk of exposure through injecting drug use and closed-setting transmission, and is a distinct action from hepatitis B/C testing, which can be completed without the vaccine also being offered. No audit in corpus of hepatitis B vaccination offer rates at prison reception (as opposed to testing) has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG57 Physical health of people in prison, rec 1.1.23 (2016)
standard.wording: Prison healthcare services (working with the NHS lead for hepatitis) should ensure that: all people are offered a hepatitis B vaccination when entering prison (for the vaccination schedule, refer to the UK Health Security Agency's Green Book).

population: All new receptions over the audit period without documented evidence of a completed hepatitis B vaccination course. Exclude people with a documented full course within the last 5 years.
sample: 40 consecutive new receptions over the last 4 weeks.
data_source: Prison electronic health record, immunisation record.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add hepatitis B vaccination as a mandatory field on the first-stage reception template, linked to an accelerated (0, 7, 21 day plus booster) schedule order set for people likely to be in custody only briefly.
reaudit: At 3 months, same reception log and template.
close_loop: Present to the prison health and justice governance board; if the mandatory field and accelerated schedule work, embed them in the establishment's standard reception pathway.
evidence: No audit in corpus of hepatitis B vaccination offer rates at prison reception.
pitfalls: Short remand stays may end before the full vaccination course is complete → use the accelerated schedule and hand over remaining doses to the community or receiving establishment on release/transfer.
Vaccination history from the community is often unverifiable → offer vaccination unless there is clear documented evidence of a completed course.
Vaccine stock and cold-chain management at reception need to be reliable → confirm supply arrangements with pharmacy before cycle 1.
Staff may conflate the vaccination offer with the separate testing offer → keep the two as distinct fields in the template to avoid double-counting.
Improvement may fade if the mandatory field is later removed in an IT update → confirm it remains mandatory at re-audit.
pearls: Recruit the prison's blood-borne virus/immunisation lead nurse as the audit lead, combining with the hepatitis B/C testing audit for efficiency.
Agree the accelerated vaccination schedule and handover process for short stays with the pharmacy and community hepatitis service before cycle 1.
Use the same reception log extraction method at re-audit.
Report vaccination offer rates at the health and justice partnership board to keep this prioritised after staff turnover.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the prison health record
pass: The reception health record documents that hepatitis B vaccination was offered, with the outcome recorded (accepted and first dose given, declined, or already fully vaccinated).

question: What proportion of people entering prison who report injecting drug use in the last month have their injection sites checked and are referred to substance misuse services if there are concerns about their immediate clinical management?
why: Injecting drug use carries specific risks (site infection, overdose, blood-borne virus transmission) that require a physical check and a clear referral pathway distinct from simply recording drug use history. No audit in corpus of injection site checking and referral completion at prison reception has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG57 Physical health of people in prison, rec 1.1.4 (table 1, item 14) (2016)
standard.wording: If the person has used intravenous drugs, check them for injection sites. Refer them to substance misuse services if there are concerns about their immediate clinical management and they need immediate support.

population: All new receptions reporting intravenous drug use in the last month over the audit period. Exclude people already actively engaged with the prison substance misuse service from a very recent previous custodial episode.
sample: 40 consecutive receptions reporting intravenous drug use over the last 6 weeks, or all if fewer.
data_source: First-stage assessment record, substance misuse service referral log.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'injection sites checked' field to the first-stage assessment template for anyone reporting intravenous drug use, with a direct one-click referral to substance misuse services built in.
reaudit: At 3 months, same reception records and template.
close_loop: Present to the prison substance misuse governance meeting; if the mandatory field and one-click referral work, embed them as the standard reception pathway for reported intravenous drug use.
evidence: No audit in corpus of injection site checking and referral completion at prison reception for people reporting intravenous drug use.
pitfalls: Disclosure of intravenous drug use may be incomplete due to stigma or fear of consequences → train staff in a non-judgemental, harm-reduction approach to improve disclosure.
Physical examination for injection sites requires appropriate privacy and consent → confirm the examination process respects dignity and consent before cycle 1.
Injection site infections may need urgent same-day medical review, not just a substance misuse referral → ensure the pathway includes an option for urgent medical assessment.
Substance misuse service capacity may limit rapid referral response → report referral-to-seen time as a secondary measure.
Improvement may fade if the mandatory field is bypassed under reception time pressure → monitor compliance at re-audit, not just presence of the field.
pearls: Recruit the prison substance misuse lead nurse and reception team jointly.
Agree the examination and consent process with the clinical lead before cycle 1.
Use the same reporting definition (intravenous drug use in the last month) at re-audit for a fair comparison.
Report results at the substance misuse governance meeting to sustain the pathway after staff turnover.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the reception record and referral log
pass: For a person reporting intravenous drug use in the last month, the record shows injection sites were physically checked, and, where there were concerns about immediate clinical management, a referral to substance misuse services was made at, or immediately after, first-stage assessment.

question: What proportion of adults with hypertension aged 80 and over on antihypertensive treatment have a clinic blood pressure below 150/90 mmHg at their most recent reading?
why: Older patients have a different, less strict blood pressure target that accounts for the balance of benefit and harm from tighter control, but this age-specific target is not always distinguished from the under-80 target in routine practice audits. No closed-loop audit in corpus specifically targets the NG136 clinic BP target for adults aged 80 and over.

standard.source: NICE NG136 Hypertension in adults: diagnosis and management, rec 1.4.21 (2019, amended 2022)
standard.wording: For adults with hypertension aged 80 and over, reduce clinic blood pressure to below 150/90 mmHg and ensure that it is maintained below that level. Use clinical judgement for people with frailty or multimorbidity.

population: Adults aged 80 and over on the practice hypertension register, on one or more antihypertensive medicines for at least 3 months, with a clinic BP reading in the last 12 months. Exclude patients with type 1 diabetes or severe CKD, who have a different NG136 table 2 target.
sample: 40 consecutive patients aged 80 and over from the hypertension register, or all if fewer.
data_source: Practice hypertension register, GP clinical system BP readings, frailty coding.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an age- and frailty-aware target display to the hypertension review template so clinicians see the correct NG136 target (under-80, 80-and-over, or individualised for frailty) automatically rather than applying a single blanket target.
reaudit: At 6 months, same register and template.
close_loop: Present at the practice's QOF/frailty meeting; if the age-aware target display improves appropriate target-setting, keep it live for all hypertension reviews.
evidence: No closed-loop audit in corpus of NG136 clinic blood pressure target achievement in adults aged 80 and over.
pitfalls: Applying the under-80 target to older patients can lead to inappropriate over-treatment and falls risk → make sure the template clearly separates the two age-based targets.
Frailty coding is often incomplete, making it hard to identify who needs an individualised target → improve frailty coding as part of this audit, not as an afterthought.
Postural hypotension should be checked in this age group per NG136 1.4.16 → include a postural BP check alongside the target assessment.
A single high reading may not reflect true control → use the most recent recorded reading but flag for re-check rather than treating one value as definitive.
Improvement may fade if the age-aware display is not maintained after an EPR update → confirm it remains accurate at re-audit.
pearls: Recruit the practice's frailty or elderly care lead GP to champion the age-aware target display.
Agree the frailty definition and individualised target-setting process with the whole team before cycle 1.
Use the same register extraction method at re-audit for a fair comparison.
Report target-achievement rates at the QOF/frailty meeting to keep this visible after the lead rotates.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the hypertension register and BP readings
pass: The most recent clinic blood pressure reading in the last 12 months is below 150/90 mmHg, or, for patients with frailty or multimorbidity, a documented clinical judgement is recorded explaining a different individualised target.

question: What proportion of stable patients with atrial fibrillation taking warfarin have their time in therapeutic range discussed, with the option of switching to a direct-acting oral anticoagulant, at their most recent routine anticoagulation review?
why: Patients remaining on warfarin despite poor anticoagulation control may benefit from switching to a DOAC, but this discussion depends on time in therapeutic range being calculated and reviewed, which is easy to omit from a routine INR check. No closed-loop audit in corpus targets this specific NG196 recommendation on warfarin review and switching.

standard.source: NICE NG196 Atrial fibrillation: diagnosis and management, rec 1.6.6 (2021)
standard.wording: For adults with atrial fibrillation who are already taking a vitamin K antagonist and are stable, continue with their current medication and discuss the option of switching treatment at their next routine appointment, taking into account the person's time in therapeutic range.

population: Adults with atrial fibrillation on warfarin under the practice's or anticoagulation clinic's routine review, with a review in the last 12 months. Exclude patients with a mechanical heart valve or other indication requiring warfarin specifically.
sample: 40 consecutive warfarin patients with a routine review in the last 12 months, or a 10% random sample if larger.
data_source: Anticoagulation clinic or practice warfarin register, INR monitoring records, consultation notes.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic time-in-therapeutic-range calculation to the anticoagulation review template, with a mandatory 'DOAC switch discussed: yes/outcome' field that cannot be left blank at routine review.
reaudit: At 6 months, same warfarin register and template.
close_loop: Present at the practice's anticoagulation/QOF meeting; if the mandatory field improves discussion rates, keep it live for every routine warfarin review.
evidence: No closed-loop audit in corpus of NG196 warfarin review and DOAC-switch discussion completion.
pitfalls: Time in therapeutic range calculation requires several recent INR results and a recognised method (for example, Rosendaal) → agree the calculation method and data source with the anticoagulation service before cycle 1.

Patients who are genuinely well controlled and prefer warfarin should still have the discussion documented, even if the outcome is to continue warfarin → audit that the discussion happened, not just the outcome.
Anticoagulation monitoring may be run by a community service outside the GP record → confirm data-sharing arrangements before starting.
Some patients have valid reasons to avoid a DOAC (for example, renal function, cost of monitoring not relevant) → record these clearly rather than treating as non-compliance.
Improvement may fade if the mandatory field is skipped when reviews are done quickly → spot-check consultation quality at re-audit.
pearls: Recruit the practice's anticoagulation lead GP or pharmacist, or the community anticoagulation service, to champion the mandatory field.
Agree the time-in-therapeutic-range calculation method before cycle 1 so results are comparable.
Use the same warfarin register extraction method at re-audit.
Report discussion completion rates at the anticoagulation/QOF meeting to sustain the pathway after the lead rotates.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the warfarin register and consultation notes
pass: At the most recent routine anticoagulation review, the patient's time in therapeutic range is calculated (or estimated from recent INR results) and a documented discussion of the option to switch to a DOAC has taken place, regardless of the outcome of that discussion.

question: What proportion of patients on the asthma register who have been dispensed 6 or more short-acting beta agonist (SABA) inhalers in the last 12 months have a documented clinical review of the reasons for overuse?
why: Heavy SABA use is a marker of poor asthma control and increased risk of a fatal or near-fatal attack, but a high dispensing count can go unnoticed if no one reviews repeat prescribing data specifically for this pattern. No closed-loop audit in corpus specifically targets clinical review triggered by SABA over-use volume (as opposed to switching the default prescribing pathway, covered elsewhere in the library).

standard.source: NICE NG245 Asthma: diagnosis, monitoring and management (BTS/NICE/SIGN), rec 1.6.1 (2024)
standard.wording: Take into account and try to address the possible reasons for uncontrolled asthma before starting or adjusting medicines for asthma in adults, young people and children. These may include: alternative diagnoses or comorbidities; suboptimal adherence; suboptimal inhaler technique; smoking (active or passive), including vaping using e-cigarettes; occupational or environmental exposures.

population: Patients aged 12 and over on the asthma register dispensed 6 or more SABA inhalers in the last 12 months, identified from the prescribing system. Exclude patients under specialist severe asthma service review with their own monitoring pathway.
sample: 40 consecutive patients meeting the SABA over-use threshold over the last 6 months, or all if fewer.
data_source: Prescribing dispensing data, asthma register, consultation templates.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Run a monthly practice search flagging patients reaching the 6-SABA-inhaler threshold, generating an automatic task for a respiratory review appointment.
reaudit: At 6 months, same prescribing search and template.
close_loop: Present at the practice's respiratory/QOF meeting; if the monthly search prompts timely review, add it to the standing list of prescribing safety searches.
evidence: No closed-loop audit in corpus of clinical review triggered by SABA over-use volume, distinct from prescribing-default switch audits already in the library.
pitfalls: Dispensing data may lag behind actual use if patients stockpile inhalers → use dispensing counts as a prompt for review, not a precise measure of use.
Patients may obtain inhalers from more than one source (for example, online pharmacy) → note this as a limitation when interpreting results.
A review may happen but not address all relevant factors → audit the content of the review, not just its occurrence.
Some patients with legitimately severe asthma may need frequent SABA under specialist guidance → exclude those under active severe asthma service review.
Improvement may fade if the monthly search stops running after a system change → confirm it is still active at re-audit.
pearls: Recruit the practice's respiratory lead nurse or pharmacist to run the monthly search and lead reviews.
Agree the 6-inhaler threshold and review template content with the team before cycle 1.
Use the same prescribing search method at re-audit for a fair comparison.
Report over-use flags and review completion at the respiratory/QOF meeting to sustain the pathway after staff rotate.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the prescribing search and consultation templates
pass: A patient dispensed 6 or more SABA inhalers in the last 12 months has a documented clinical review addressing possible reasons for overuse (inhaler technique, adherence, alternative diagnoses, smoking/vaping, triggers) within 8 weeks of reaching that threshold.

question: What proportion of adults with a new diagnosis of chronic kidney disease have their GFR and ACR category jointly recorded and used to state their risk of adverse outcomes in the record?
why: NICE's CKD classification combines GFR and ACR categories into a single risk grid, but practices commonly record the two results without translating them into the combined risk category that should guide monitoring frequency and referral. No closed-loop audit in corpus targets whether the combined GFR/ACR risk classification (as opposed to the individual test results) is documented.

standard.source: NICE NG203 Chronic kidney disease: assessment and management, rec 1.2.1 (2014)
standard.wording: Classify CKD in adults using a combination of GFR and ACR categories (as described in table 1). Be aware that: increased ACR is associated with increased risk of adverse outcomes; decreased GFR is associated with increased risk of adverse outcomes; increased ACR and decreased GFR in combination multiply the risk of adverse outcomes.

population: Adults with a coded diagnosis of CKD (stage 3a or above, or stage 1-2 with proteinuria) with a GFR and ACR result in the last 12 months. Exclude patients under active nephrology follow-up whose classification is documented in specialist correspondence rather than the GP record.
sample: 40 consecutive patients from the CKD register, or a 10% random sample if larger.
data_source: CKD register, GP clinical system, laboratory results, annual review template.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic GFR/ACR risk-grid calculator to the CKD annual review template that displays the combined NICE risk category as soon as both results are entered, rather than requiring manual look-up of table 1.
reaudit: At 6 months, same register and template.
close_loop: Present at the practice's QOF/long-term conditions meeting; if the automatic calculator improves documentation, keep it as the default CKD annual review tool.
evidence: No closed-loop audit in corpus of combined GFR/ACR risk classification documentation under NG203 rec 1.2.1.
pitfalls: GFR and ACR results may be recorded on different dates and never brought together in one place → the calculator should pull the most recent value of each, regardless of date, and flag if either is more than 12 months old.
Staff may record the individual numeric results without translating them into the categorical grid → make the categorical output, not just the raw numbers, the audited item.
Patients under nephrology may have their classification documented only in hospital letters → check for this before counting as a gap in the GP record.
A single ACR result in category A2/A3 needs confirmation before acting on it clinically, per NICE → note this distinction in staff training so classification and clinical action are not conflated.
Improvement may fade if the calculator is not maintained after an EPR template change → confirm it remains functional at re-audit.
pearls: Recruit the practice's CKD lead nurse or clinical pharmacist to champion the automatic calculator.
Agree the calculator's exact grid values with NICE table 1 before building it, to avoid errors.
Use the same CKD register definition at re-audit for a fair comparison.
Report documentation rates at the QOF/long-term conditions meeting to keep this visible after the lead rotates.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the CKD register and laboratory results
pass: The record documents both the GFR category (G1-G5) and ACR category (A1-A3) together, with the combined NICE risk category (low, moderate, high or very high) stated, at the time of diagnosis or most recent annual review.

question: What proportion of patients on shared-care DMARD monitoring have their individual risk factors for toxicity (renal function, age, alcohol use, interacting medicines) reviewed at least annually, with monitoring frequency adjusted accordingly?
why: DMARD shared care guidance expects monitoring frequency to be individualised to risk, not applied as a single fixed interval for everyone, but an annual risk review distinct from the routine blood test cycle is easy to omit. No closed-loop audit in corpus targets the annual DMARD toxicity risk review as a discrete step separate from routine blood monitoring.

standard.source: British Society for Rheumatology shared care guidance for DMARD monitoring (as summarised by NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service)
standard.wording: Risk factors for DMARD toxicity should be reviewed at least annually, adjusting the frequency of monitoring according to the level of risk identified. A shared care protocol should be agreed upon delineating the responsibilities of each party.

population: Patients on the practice's shared-care DMARD register on treatment for 12 months or more. Exclude patients within their first year of treatment, who follow a different, more frequent initial monitoring schedule.
sample: 40 consecutive patients on the shared-care DMARD register on treatment for over 12 months, or all if fewer.
data_source: Shared-care DMARD register, GP consultation and annual review templates, laboratory results.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a dedicated 'annual DMARD risk review' template, separate from the routine blood monitoring recall, that prompts the reviewing clinician to check renal trend, age, alcohol use and new interacting prescriptions once a year for every shared-care DMARD patient.
reaudit: At 12 months, same register and template.
close_loop: Present at the practice's medicines optimisation/QOF meeting; if the dedicated template improves completion, keep it as a standing annual task alongside routine monitoring.
evidence: No closed-loop audit in corpus of the annual DMARD toxicity risk review as a discrete step from routine blood monitoring.
pitfalls: Routine blood monitoring can be mistaken for the full annual risk review, when it only covers some of the required factors → keep the two as clearly separate template items.

Interacting medicines (for example, trimethoprim prescribed by an out-of-hours service) may not trigger an alert if prescribed outside the practice → include a manual interaction check as part of the annual review.
Alcohol intake may be under-reported → use a standard, non-judgemental question as part of the review.
Shared care responsibilities between specialist and GP may be unclear for who leads the annual risk review → confirm this explicitly in the shared care agreement before cycle 1.
Improvement may fade if the annual review template is not linked to a recall system → build in an automatic annual reminder.
pearls: Recruit the practice's clinical pharmacist to lead the annual risk review process.
Agree with the rheumatology or gastroenterology shared care team which factors and thresholds to use before cycle 1.
Use the same DMARD register definitions at re-audit for a fair comparison.
Report annual review completion at the medicines optimisation meeting to sustain the process after staff rotate.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the DMARD register and consultation templates
pass: A documented annual review of individual toxicity risk factors (renal function trend, age, alcohol intake, interacting medicines such as trimethoprim or NSAIDs) is recorded, with the monitoring interval confirmed as appropriate or adjusted as a result.
